entries.107e4b5956d57fa04ca59e8544110738e1f31e18: <div sID="gen31694" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Gal.3" sID="Gal.3"/> <div eID="gen31694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31695" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31696" type="x-p"/> The apostle in this chapter, I. Reproves the Galatians for their folly, in suffering themselves to be drawn away from the faith of the gospel, and endeavours, from several considerations, to impress them with a sense of it. II. He proves the doctrine which he had reproved them for departing from—that of justification by faith without the works of the law, 1. From the example of Abraham's justification. 2. From the nature and tenour of the law. 3. From the express testimony of the Old Testament; and, 4. From the stability of the covenant of God with Abraham. Lest any should hereupon say, "Wherefore then serveth the law?" he answers, (1.) It was added because of transgressions. (2.) It was given to convince the world of the necessity of a Saviour. (3.) It was designed as a schoolmaster, to bring us to Christ. And then he concludes the chapter by acquainting us with the privilege of Christians under the gospel state.
entries.58917de297b84f52c3cb2e541b819a4bc9bb7ff8: <div eID="gen31696" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31695" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Justification by Faith. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31697" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you? <hi type="super">2</hi> This only would I learn of you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? <hi type="super">3</hi> Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh? 4 Have ye suffered so many things in vain? if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> yet in vain. <hi type="super">5</hi> He therefore that ministereth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles among you, <hi type="italic">doeth he it</hi> by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? <div eID="gen31697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31698" type="x-p"/> The apostle is here dealing with those who, having embraced the faith of Christ, still continued to seek for justification by the works of the law; that is, who depended upon their own obedience to the moral precepts as their righteousness before God, and, wherein that was defective, had recourse to the legal sacrifices and purifications to make it up. These he first sharply reproves, and then endeavours, by the evidence of truth, to convince them. This is the right method, when we reprove any for a fault or an error, to convince them that it is an error, that it is a fault. <div eID="gen31698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31699" type="x-p"/> He reproves them, and the reproof is very close and warm: he calls them <hi type="italic">foolish Galatians,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Though as Christians they were Wisdom's children, yet as corrupt Christians they were foolish children. Yea, he asks, <hi type="italic">Who hath bewitched you?</hi> whereby he represents them as enchanted by the arts and snares of their seducing teachers, and so far deluded as to act very unlike themselves. That wherein their folly and infatuation appeared was that <hi type="italic">they did not obey the truth;</hi> that is, they did not adhere to the gospel way of justification, wherein they had been taught, and which they had professed to embrace. Note, It is not enough to know the truth, and to say we believe it, but we must obey it too; we must heartily submit to it, and stedfastly abide by it. Note, also, Those are spiritually bewitched who, when the truth as it is in Jesus is plainly set before them, will not thus obey it. Several things proved and aggravated the folly of these Christians. <div eID="gen31699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31700" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ had been evidently set forth as crucified among them;</hi> that is, they had had the doctrine of the cross preached to them, and the sacrament of the Lord's supper administered among them, in both which Christ crucified had been set before them. Now, it was the greatest madness that could be for those who had acquaintance with such sacred mysteries, and admittance to such great solemnities, not to obey the truth which was thus published to them, and signed and sealed in that ordinance. Note, The consideration of the honours and privileges we have been admitted to as Christians should shame us out of the folly of apostasy and backsliding. <div eID="gen31700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31701" type="x-p"/> 2. He appeals to the experiences they had had of the working of the Spirit upon their souls (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.2">v. 2</reference>); he puts them in mind that, upon their becoming Christians, <hi type="italic">they had received the Spirit,</hi> that many of them at least had been made partakers not only of the sanctifying influences, but of the miraculous gifts, of the Holy Spirit, which were eminent proofs of the truth of the Christian religion and the several doctrines of it, and especially of this, that justification is by Christ only, and not by the works of the law, which was one of the peculiar and fundamental principles of it. To convince them of the folly of their departing from this doctrine, he desires to know how they came by these gifts and graces: Was it <hi type="italic">by the works of the law,</hi> that is, the preaching of the necessity of these in order to justification? This they could not say, for that doctrine had not then been preached to them, nor had they, as Gentiles, any pretence to justification in that way. Or was it by the <hi type="italic">hearing of faith,</hi> that is, the preaching of the doctrine of faith in Christ as the only way of justification? This, if they would say the truth, they were obliged to own, and therefore must be very unreasonable if they should reject a doctrine of the good effects of which they had had such experience. Note, (1.) It is usually by the ministry of the gospel that the Spirit is communicated to persons. And, (2.) Those are very unwise who suffer themselves to be turned away from the ministry and doctrine which have been blessed to their spiritual advantage. <div eID="gen31701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31702" type="x-p"/> 3. He calls upon them to consider their past and present conduct, and thence to judge whether they were not acting very weakly and unreasonably (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.3-Gal.3.4">v. 3, 4</reference>): he tells them that <hi type="italic">they had begun in the Spirit,</hi> but now were seeking <hi type="italic">to be made perfect by the flesh;</hi> they had embraced the doctrine of the gospel, by means of which they had received the Spirit, and wherein only the true way of justification is revealed. And thus they had begun well; but now they were turning to the law, and expected to be advanced to higher degrees of perfection by adding the observance of it to faith in Christ, in order to their justification, which could end in nothing but their shame and disappointment: for this, instead of being an improvement upon the gospel, was really a perversion of it; and, while they sought to be justified in this way, they were so far from being more perfect Christians that they were more in danger of becoming no Christians at all; hereby they were pulling down with one hand what they had built with the other, and undoing what they had hitherto done in Christianity. Yea, he further puts them in mind that they had not only embraced the Christian doctrine, but suffered for it too; and therefore their folly would be the more aggravated, if now they should desert it: for in this case all that they had suffered would be in vain—it would appear that they had been foolish in suffering for what they now deserted, and their sufferings would be altogether in vain, and of no advantage to them. Note, (1.) It is the folly of apostates that they lose the benefit of all they have done in religion, or suffered for it. And, (2.) It is very sad for any to live in an age of services and sufferings, of sabbaths, sermons, and sacraments, in vain; in this case former righteousness shall not be mentioned. <div eID="gen31702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31703" type="x-p"/> 4. He puts them in mind that they had had ministers among them (and particularly himself) who came with a divine seal and commission; for they had <hi type="italic">ministered the Spirit to them, and wrought miracles among them:</hi> and he appeals to them whether they did it <hi type="italic">by the works of the law or by the hearing of faith,</hi> whether the doctrine that was preached by them, and confirmed by the miraculous gifts and operations of the Spirit, was that of justification by the works of the law or by the faith of Christ; they very well knew that it was not the former, but the latter; and therefore must needs be inexcusable in forsaking a doctrine which had been so signally owned and attested, and exchanging it for one that had received no such attestations.
entries.0f3d56b79eb263dad02c042a675588de77f2da1a: <div eID="gen31703" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Justification by Faith. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31704" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. <hi type="super">7</hi> Know ye therefore that they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham. 8 And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> In thee shall all nations be blessed. <hi type="super">9</hi> So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham. 10 For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed <hi type="italic">is</hi> every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them. <hi type="super">11</hi> But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> evident: for, The just shall live by faith. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them. <hi type="super">13</hi> Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed <hi type="italic">is</hi> every one that hangeth on a tree: <hi type="super">14</hi> That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. <hi type="super">15</hi> Brethren, I speak after the manner of men; Though <hi type="italic">it be</hi> but a man's covenant, yet <hi type="italic">if it be</hi> confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto. <hi type="super">16</hi> Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ. 17 And this I say, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect. <hi type="super">18</hi> For if the inheritance <hi type="italic">be</hi> of the law, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> no more of promise: but God gave <hi type="italic">it</hi> to Abraham by promise. <div eID="gen31704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31705" type="x-p"/> The apostle having reproved the Galatians for not obeying the truth, and endeavoured to impress them with a sense of their folly herein, in these verses he largely proves the doctrine which he had reproved them for rejecting, namely, that of justification by faith without the works of the law. This he does several ways. <div eID="gen31705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31706" type="x-p"/> I. From the example of Abraham's justification. This argument the apostle uses, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.1-Rom.4.25">Rom. iv</reference>. <hi type="italic">Abraham believed God, and that was accounted to him for righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.6">v. 6</reference>); that is, his faith fastened upon the word and promise of God, and upon his believing he was owned and accepted of God as a righteous man: as on this account he is represented as the father of the faithful, so the apostle would have us to know <hi type="italic">that those who are of faith are the children of Abraham</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.7">v. 7</reference>), not according to the flesh, but according to the promise; and, consequently, that they are justified in the same way that he was. Abraham was justified by faith, and so are they. To confirm this, the apostle acquaints us that the promise made to Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen. xii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">In thee shall all nations be blessed,</hi> had a reference hereunto, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.8">v. 8</reference>. The scripture is said to <hi type="italic">foresee,</hi> because he that indited the scripture did foresee, that God would justify the heathen world in the way of faith; and therefore in Abraham, that is, in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, not the Jews only, but the Gentiles also, should be blessed; not only blessed in the seed of Abraham, but blessed as Abraham was, being justified as he was. This the apostle calls <hi type="italic">preaching the gospel to Abraham;</hi> and thence infers (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.9">v. 9</reference>) that <hi type="italic">those who are of faith,</hi> that is, true believers, of what nation soever they are, <hi type="italic">are blessed with faithful Abraham.</hi> They are blessed with Abraham the father of the faithful, by the promise made to him, and therefore by faith as he was. It was through faith in the promise of God that he was blessed, and it is only in the same way that others obtain this privilege. <div eID="gen31706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31707" type="x-p"/> II. He shows that we cannot be justified but by faith fastening on the gospel, because the law condemns us. If we put ourselves upon trial in that court, and stand to the sentence of it, we are certainly cast, and lost, and undone; <hi type="italic">for as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse,</hi> as many as depend upon the merit of their own works as their righteousness, as plead not guilty, and insist upon their own justification, the cause will certainly go against them; <hi type="italic">for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">v. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">and Deut. xxvii. 26</reference>. The condition of life, by the law, is perfect, personal, and perpetual, obedience; the language of it is, <hi type="italic">Do this and live;</hi> or, as <reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">v. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">The man that doeth them shall live in them:</hi> and for every failure herein the law denounces a curse. Unless our obedience be universal, continuing in all things that are written in the book of the law, and unless it be perpetual too (if in any instance at any time we fail and come short), we fall under the curse of the law. The curse is wrath revealed, and ruin threatened: it is a separation unto all evil, and this is in full force, power, and virtue, against all sinners, and therefore against all men; for all have sinned and become guilty before God: and if, as transgressors of the law, we are under the curse of it, it must be a vain thing to look for justification by it. But, though this is not to be expected from the law, yet the apostle afterwards acquaints us that there is a way open to our escaping this curse, and regaining the favour of God, namely, through faith in Christ, who (as he says, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">v. 13</reference>) <hi type="italic">hath redeemed us from the curse of the law,</hi> &c. A strange method it was which Christ took to redeem us from the curse of the law; it was <hi type="italic">by his being himself made a curse for us.</hi> Being made sin for us, he was made a curse for us; not separated from God, but laid for the present under that infamous token of the divine displeasure upon which the law of Moses had put a particular brand, <reference osisRef="Deut.21.22">Deut. xxi. 22</reference>. The design of this was <hi type="italic">that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ</hi>—that all who believed on Christ, whether Jews or Gentiles, might become heirs of Abraham's blessing, and particularly of that great promise of the Spirit, which was peculiarly reserved for the times of the gospel. Hence it appeared that it was not by putting themselves under the law, but by faith in Christ, that they become the people of God and heirs of the promise. Here note, 1. The misery which as sinners we are sunk into—we are under the curse and condemnation of the law. 2. The love and grace of our Lord Jesus Christ towards us—he has submitted to be made a curse for us, that he might redeem us from the curse of the law. 3. The happy prospect which we now have through him, not only of escaping the curse, but of inheriting the blessing. And, 4. That it is only through faith in him that we can hope to obtain this favour. <div eID="gen31707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31708" type="x-p"/> III. To prove that justification is by faith, and not by the works of the law, the apostle alleges the express testimony of the Old Testament, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.11">v. 11</reference>. The place referred to is <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Habak. ii. 4</reference>, where it is said, <hi type="italic">The just shall live by faith;</hi> it is again quoted, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Rom. i. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">and Heb. x. 38</reference>. The design of it is to show that those only are just or righteous who do truly live, who are freed from death and wrath, and restored into a state of life in the favour of God; and that it is only through faith that persons become righteous, and as such obtain this life and happiness—that they are accepted of God, and enabled to live to him now, and are entitled to an eternal life in the enjoyment of him hereafter. Hence the apostle says, <hi type="italic">It is evident that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God.</hi> Whatever he may be in the account of others, yet he is not so in the sight of God; for <hi type="italic">the law is not of faith</hi>—that says nothing concerning faith in the business of justification, nor does it give life to those who believe; but the language of it is, <hi type="italic">The man that doeth them shall live in them,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Lev. xviii. 5</reference>. It requires perfect obedience as the condition of life, and therefore now can by no means be the rule of our justification. This argument of the apostle's may give us occasion to remark that justification by faith is no new doctrine, but what was established and taught in the church of God long before the times of the gospel. Yea, it is the only way wherein any sinners ever were, or can be, justified. <div eID="gen31708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31709" type="x-p"/> IV. To this purpose the apostle urges the stability of the covenant which God made with Abraham, which was not vacated nor disannulled by the giving of the law to Moses, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.15">v. 15</reference>, &c. Faith had the precedence of the law, for Abraham was justified by faith. It was a promise that he built upon, and promises are the proper objects of faith. God entered into covenant with Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.8">v. 8</reference>), and this covenant was firm and steady; even men's covenants are so, and therefore much more his. When a deed is executed, or articles of agreement are sealed, both parties are bound, and it is too late then to settle things otherwise; and therefore it is not to be supposed that by the subsequent law the covenant of God should be vacated. The original word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">diatheke</hi></hi> signifies both a covenant and a testament. Now the promise made to Abraham was rather a testament than a covenant. When a testament has become of force by the death of the testator, it is not capable of being altered; and therefore, the promise that was given to Abraham being of the nature of a testament, it remains firm and unalterable. But, if it should be said that a grant or testament may be defeated for want of persons to claim the benefit of it (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">v. 16</reference>), he shows that there is no danger of that in this case. Abraham is dead, and the prophets are dead, but the covenant is made with Abraham and his seed. And he gives us a very surprising exposition of this. We should have thought it had been meant only of the people of the Jews. "Nay," says the apostle, "it is in the singular number, and points at a single person—<hi type="italic">that seed is Christ,</hi>" So that the covenant is still in force; for Christ abideth for ever in his person, and in his spiritual seed, who are his by faith. And if it be objected that the law which was given by Moses did disannul this covenant, because that insisted so much upon works, and there was so little in it of faith or of the promised Messiah, he answers that the subsequent law could not disannul the previous covenant or promise (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">If the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise; but,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">God gave it to Abraham by promise,</hi> and therefore it would be inconsistent with his holiness, wisdom, and faithfulness, by any subsequent act to set aside the promise, and so alter the way of justification which he had thus established. If the inheritance was given to Abraham by promise, and thereby entailed upon his spiritual seed, we may be sure that God would not retract that promise; for he is not a man that he should repent.
entries.9e9ed7649f18c5954d73c60a304ffee3dd4a72de: <div eID="gen31709" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Design of the Law; The True Children of Abraham. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31710" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Wherefore then <hi type="italic">serveth</hi> the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made; <hi type="italic">and it was</hi> ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. <hi type="super">20</hi> Now a mediator is not <hi type="italic">a mediator</hi> of one, but God is one. <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> the law then against the promises of God? God forbid: for if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law. <hi type="super">22</hi> But the scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe. <hi type="super">23</hi> But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed. <hi type="super">24</hi> Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster <hi type="italic">to bring us</hi> unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. <hi type="super">25</hi> But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. <hi type="super">26</hi> For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">27</hi> For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. <hi type="super">28</hi> There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">29</hi> And if ye <hi type="italic">be</hi> Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise. <div eID="gen31710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31711" type="x-p"/> The apostle having just before been speaking of the promise made to Abraham, and representing that as the rule of our justification, and not the law, lest they should think he did too much derogate from the law, and render it altogether useless, he thence takes occasion to discourse of the design and tendency of it, and to acquaint us for what purposes it was given. It might be asked, "If that promise be sufficient for salvation, wherefore then serveth the law? Or, Why did God give the law by Moses?" To this he answers, <div eID="gen31711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31712" type="x-p"/> I. The law <hi type="italic">was added because of transgressions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">v. 19</reference>. It was not designed to disannul the promise, and to establish a different way of justification from that which was settled by the promise; but <hi type="italic">it was added</hi> to it, annexed on purpose to be subservient to it, and it was so <hi type="italic">because of transgressions.</hi> The Israelites, though they were chosen to be God's peculiar people, were sinners as well as others, and therefore the law was given to convince them of their sin, and of their obnoxiousness to the divine displeasure on the account of it; <hi type="italic">for by the law is the knowledge of sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.20">Rom. iii. 20</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the law entered that sin might abound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Rom. v. 20</reference>. And it was also intended to restrain them from the commission of sin, to put an awe upon their minds, and be a curb upon their lusts, that they should not run into that excess of riot to which they were naturally inclined; and yet at the same time it was designed to direct them to the true and only way whereby sin was to be expiated, and wherein they might obtain the pardon of it; namely, through the death and sacrifice of Christ, which was the special use for which the law of sacrifices and purifications was given. <div eID="gen31712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31713" type="x-p"/> The apostle adds that the law was given for this purpose <hi type="italic">till the seed should come to whom the promise was made;</hi> that is, either till Christ should come (the principle seed referred to in the promise, as he had before shown), or till the gospel dispensation should take place, when Jews and Gentiles, without distinction, should, upon believing, become the seed of Abraham. The law was added because of transgressions, till this fulness of time, or this complete dispensation, should come. But when the seed came, and a fuller discovery of divine grace in the promise was made, then the law, as given by Moses, was to cease; that covenant, being found faulty, was to give place to another, and a better, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.7-Heb.8.8">Heb. viii. 7, 8</reference>. And though the law, considered as the law of nature, is always in force, and still continues to be of use to convince men of sin and to restrain them from it, yet we are now no longer under the bondage and terror of that legal covenant. The law then was not intended to discover another way of justification, different from that revealed by the promise, but only to lead men to see their need of the promise, by showing them the sinfulness of sin, and to point them to Christ, through whom alone they could be pardoned and justified. <div eID="gen31713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31714" type="x-p"/> As a further proof that the law was not designed to vacate the promise, the apostle adds, <hi type="italic">It was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator.</hi> It was given to different persons, and in a different manner from the promise, and therefore for different purposes. The promise was made to Abraham, and all his spiritual seed, including believers of all nations, even of the Gentiles as well as the Jews; but the law was given to the Israelites as a peculiar people, and separated from the rest of the world. And, whereas the promise was given immediately by God himself, the law was given <hi type="italic">by the ministry of angels, and the hand of a mediator.</hi> Hence it appeared that the law could not be designed to set aside the promise; for (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">A mediator is not a mediator of one,</hi> of one party only; <hi type="italic">but God is one,</hi> but one party in the promise or covenant made with Abraham: and therefore it is not to be supposed that by a transaction which passed only between him and the nation of the Jews he should make void a promise which he had long before made to Abraham and all his spiritual seed, whether Jews or Gentiles. This would not have been consistent with his wisdom, nor with his truth and faithfulness. Moses was only a mediator between God and the spiritual seed of Abraham; and therefore the law that was given by him could not affect the promise made to them, much less be subversive of it. <div eID="gen31714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31715" type="x-p"/> II. The law was given to convince men of the necessity of a Saviour. The apostle asks (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">v. 21</reference>), as what some might be willing to object, "<hi type="italic">Is the law then against the promises of God?</hi> Do they really clash and interfere with each other? Or do you not set the covenant with Abraham, and the law of Moses, at variance with one another?" To this he answers, <hi type="italic">God forbid;</hi> he was far from entertaining such a thought, nor could it be inferred from what he had said. The law is by no means inconsistent with the promise, but subservient to it, as the design of it is to discover men's transgressions, and to show them the need they have of a better righteousness than that of the law. That consequence would much rather follow from their doctrine than from his; <hi type="italic">for, if there had been a law given that could have given life, verily righteousness would have been by the law,</hi> and in that case the promise would have been superseded and rendered useless. But that in our present state could not be, <hi type="italic">for the scripture hath concluded all under sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.22">v. 22</reference>), or declared that all, both Jew and Gentile, are in a state of guilt, and therefore unable to attain to righteousness and justification by the works of the law. The law discovered their wounds, but could not afford them a remedy: it showed that they were guilty, because it appointed sacrifices and purifications, which were manifestly insufficient to take away sin: and therefore the great design of it was <hi type="italic">that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those that believe,</hi> that being convinced of their guilt, and the insufficiency of the law to effect a righteousness for them, they might be persuaded to believe on Christ, and so obtain the benefit of the promise. <div eID="gen31715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31716" type="x-p"/> III. The law was designed for <hi type="italic">a schoolmaster, to bring men to Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.24">v. 24</reference>. In the <reference osisRef="Gal.3.23">foregoing verse</reference>, the apostle acquaints us with the state of the Jews under the Mosaic economy, that <hi type="italic">before faith came,</hi> or before Christ appeared and the doctrine of justification by faith in him was more fully discovered, <hi type="italic">they were kept under the law,</hi> obliged, under severe penalties, to a strict observance of the various precepts of it; and at that time they were shut up, held under the terror and discipline of it, as prisoners in a state of confinement: the design of this was that hereby they might be disposed more readily to embrace <hi type="italic">the faith which should afterwards be revealed,</hi> or be persuaded to accept Christ when he came into the world, and to fall in with that better dispensation he was to introduce, whereby they were to be freed from bondage and servitude, and brought into a state of greater light and liberty. Now, in that state, he tells them, <hi type="italic">the law was their schoolmaster, to bring them to Christ, that they might be justified by faith.</hi> As it declared the mind and will of God concerning them, and at the same time denounced a curse against them for every failure in their duty, so it was proper to convince them of their lost and undone condition in themselves, and to let them see the weakness and insufficiency of their own righteousness to recommend them to God. And as it obliged them to a variety of sacrifices, &c., which, though they could not of themselves take away sin, were typical of Christ, and of the great sacrifice which he was to offer up for the expiation of it, so it directed them (though in a more dark and obscure manner) to him as their only relief and refuge. And thus it was their schoolmaster, to instruct and govern them in their state of minority, or, as the word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">paidagogos</hi></hi> most properly signifies, their <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> to lead and conduct them to Christ (as children were wont to be led to school by those servants who had the care of them); that they might be more fully instructed by him as their schoolmaster, in the true way of justification and salvation, which is only by faith in him, and of which he was appointed to give the fullest and clearest discoveries. But lest it should be said, If the law was of this use and service under the Jewish, why may it not continue to be so under the Christian state too, the apostle adds (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.25">v. 25</reference>) that <hi type="italic">after faith has come,</hi> and the gospel dispensation has taken place, under which Christ, and the way of pardon and life through faith in him, are set in the clearest light, <hi type="italic">we are no longer under a schoolmaster</hi>—we have no such need of the law to direct us to him as there was then. Thus the apostle acquaints us for what uses and purposes the law served; and, from what he says concerning this matter, we may observe, <div eID="gen31716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31717" type="x-p"/> 1. The goodness of God to his people of old, in giving the law to them; for though, in comparison of the gospel state, it was a dispensation of darkness and terror, yet it furnished them with sufficient means and helps both to direct them in their duty to God and to encourage their hopes in him. <div eID="gen31717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31718" type="x-p"/> 2. The great fault and folly of the Jews, in mistaking the design of the law, and abusing it to a very different purpose from that which God intended in the giving of it; for they expected to be justified by the works of it, whereas it was never designed to be the rule of their justification, but only a means of convincing them of their guilt and of their need of a Saviour, and of directing them to Christ, and faith in him, as the only way of obtaining this privilege. See <reference osisRef="Rom.9.31-Rom.9.32">Rom. ix. 31, 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3-Rom.10.4">x. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen31718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31719" type="x-p"/> 3. The great advantage of the gospel state above the legal, under which we not only enjoy a clearer discovery of divine grace and mercy than was afforded to the Jews of old, but are also freed from the state of bondage and terror under which they were held. We are not now treated as children in a state of minority, but as sons grown up to a full age, who are admitted to greater freedoms, and instated in larger privileges, than they were. This the apostle enlarges upon in the <reference osisRef="Gal.3.26-Gal.3.29">following verses</reference>. For, having shown for what intent the law was given, in the close of the chapter he acquaints us with our privilege by Christ, where he particularly declares, <div eID="gen31719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31720" type="x-p"/> (1.) That <hi type="italic">we are the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.26">v. 26</reference>. And here we may observe, [1.] The great and excellent privilege which real Christians enjoy under the gospel: <hi type="italic">They are the children of God;</hi> they are no longer accounted servants, but <hi type="italic">sons;</hi> they are not now kept at such a distance, and under such restraints, as the Jews were, but are allowed a nearer and freer access to God than was granted to them; yea, they are admitted into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of his children. [2.] How they come to obtain this privilege, and that is <hi type="italic">by faith in Christ Jesus.</hi> Having accepted him as their Lord and Saviour, and relying on him alone for justification and salvation, they are hereupon admitted into this happy relation to God, and are entitled to the privileges of it; for (<reference osisRef="John.1.12">John i. 12</reference>) <hi type="italic">as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to those that believe on his name.</hi> And this faith in Christ, whereby they became the children of God, he reminds us (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.27">v. 27</reference>), was what they professed in baptism; for he adds, <hi type="italic">As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.</hi> Having in baptism professed their faith in him, they were thereby devoted to him, and had, as it were, put on his livery, and declared themselves to be his servants and disciples; and having thus become the members of Christ, they were through him owned and accounted as the children of God. Here note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Baptism is now the solemn rite of our admission into the Christian church, as circumcision was into that of the Jews. Our Lord Jesus appointed it to be so, in the commission he gave to his apostles (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.19">Matt. xxviii. 19</reference>), and accordingly it was their practice to baptize those whom they had discipled to the Christian faith; and perhaps the apostle might take notice of their baptism here, and of their becoming the children of God through faith in Christ, professed therein, to obviate a further objection, which the false teachers might be apt to urge in favour of circumcision. They might be ready to say, "Though it should be allowed that the law, as given at mount Sinai, was abrogated by the coming of Christ the promised seed, yet why should circumcision be set aside too, when that was given to Abraham together with the promise, and long before the giving of the law by Moses?" But this difficulty is sufficiently removed when the apostle says, <hi type="italic">Those who are baptized into Christ have put on Christ;</hi> for thence it appears that under the gospel baptism comes in the room of circumcision, and that those who by baptism are devoted to Christ, and do sincerely believe in him, are to all intents and purposes as much admitted into the privileges of the Christian state as the Jews were by circumcision into those of the legal (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Phil. iii. 3</reference>), and therefore there was no reason why the use of that should still be continued. Note, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In our baptism we put on Christ; therein we profess our discipleship to him, and are obliged to behave ourselves as his faithful servants. Being baptized into Christ, we are baptized into his death, that as he died and rose again, so, in conformity thereunto, we should die unto sin, and walk in newness of life (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.3-Rom.6.4">Rom. vi. 3, 4</reference>); it would be of great advantage to us did we oftener remember this. <div eID="gen31720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31721" type="x-p"/> (2.) That this privilege of being the children of God, and of being by baptism devoted to Christ, is now enjoyed in common by all real Christians. The law indeed made a difference between Jew and Greek, giving the Jews on many accounts the pre-eminence: that also made a difference between <hi type="italic">bond and free,</hi> master and servant, and between <hi type="italic">male and female,</hi> the males being circumcised. But it is not so now; they all stand on the same level, <hi type="italic">and are all one in Christ Jesus;</hi> as the one is not accepted on the account of any national or personal advantages he may enjoy above the other, so neither is the other rejected for the want of them; but all who sincerely believe on Christ, of what nation, or sex, or condition, soever they be, are accepted of him, and become the children of God through faith in him. <div eID="gen31721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31722" type="x-p"/> (3.) That, <hi type="italic">being Christ's, we are Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise.</hi> Their judaizing teachers would have them believe that they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, or they could not be saved: "No," says the apostle, "there is no need of that; for <hi type="italic">if you be Christ's,</hi> if you sincerely believe on him, who is the promised seed, in whom all the nations of the earth were to be blessed, you therefore become the true <hi type="italic">seed of Abraham,</hi> the father of the faithful, and as such <hi type="italic">are heirs according to the promise,</hi> and consequently are entitled to the great blessings and privileges of it." And therefore upon the whole, since it appeared that justification was not to be attained by the works of the law, but only by faith in Christ, and that the law of Moses was a temporary institution and was given for such purposes as were only subservient to and not subversive of the promise, and that now, under the gospel, Christians enjoy much greater and better privileges than the Jews did under that dispensation, it must needs follow that they were very unreasonable and unwise, in hearkening to those who at once endeavoured to deprive them of the truth and liberty of the gospel.  <chapter eID="Gal.3"/> <div eID="gen31722" type="x-p"/>

entries.78d521768115a9e34116735f752cf6683df0bc22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17467"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gal.3.1-Gal.3.29">Ga 3:1-29</reference>. Reproof of the Galatians for Abandoning Faith for Legalism. Justification by Faith Vindicated: The Law Shown to Be Subsequent to the Promise: Believers Are the Spiritual Seed of Abraham, Who Was Justified by Faith. The Law Was Our Schoolmaster to Bring Us to Christ, that We Might Become Children of God by Faith.</title> <div sID="gen35012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17467"/><hi type="bold">1. that ye should not obey the truth--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen35012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bewitched--</hi>fascinated you so that you have lost your wits. Themistius says the Galatians were naturally very acute in intellect. Hence, Paul wonders they could be so misled in this case.<div eID="gen35013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">you--</hi>emphatical. "You, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been graphically set forth (literally, in writing, namely, by vivid portraiture in preaching) among you, crucified" (so the sense and Greek order require rather than English Version). As Christ was "crucified," so ye ought to have been by faith "crucified with Christ," and so "dead to the law" (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.19">Ga 2:19</reference>, 20). Reference to the "eyes" is appropriate, as fascination was supposed to be exercised through the eyes. The sight of Christ crucified ought to have been enough to counteract all fascination. <div eID="gen35014" type="x-p"/>
entries.099d6576f664f9f1fbb31ea6a172243e7ce9d1ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17468"/><div sID="gen35015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17468"/>2. "Was it by the works of the law that ye received the Spirit (manifested by outward miracles, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.5">Ga 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.16.17">Mr 16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.4">He 2:4</reference>; and by spiritual graces, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Ga 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.5">Ga 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>), or by the hearing of faith?" The "only" implies, "I desire, omitting other arguments, to rest the question on this alone"; I who was your teacher, desire now to "learn" this one thing from you. The epithet "Holy" is not prefixed to "Spirit" because that epithet is a joyous one, whereas this Epistle is stern and reproving [Bengel].<div eID="gen35015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hearing of faith--</hi>Faith consists not in working, but in receiving (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.16">Ro 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen35016" type="x-p"/>
entries.7fa0bb9383dc418b6977785b8407e2e69e77f3de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17469"/><div sID="gen35017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17469"/><hi type="bold">3. begun--</hi>the Christian life (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Php 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen35017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Spirit--</hi>Not merely was Christ crucified "graphically set forth" in my preaching, but also "the Spirit" confirmed the word preached, by imparting His spiritual gifts. "Having thus begun" with the receiving His spiritual gifts, "are ye now being made perfect" (so the Greek), that is, are ye seeking to be made perfect with "fleshly" ordinances of the law? [Estius]. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.2.28">Ro 2:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Php 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">He 9:10</reference>. Having begun in the Spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit ruling your spiritual life as its "essence and active principle" [Ellicott], in contrast to "the flesh," the element in which the law works [Alford]. Having begun your Christianity in the Spirit, that is, in the divine life that proceeds from faith, are ye seeking after something higher still (the perfecting of your Christianity) in the sensuous and the earthly, which cannot possibly elevate the inner life of the Spirit, namely, outward ceremonies? [Neander]. No doubt the Galatians thought that they were going more deeply into the Spirit; for the flesh may be easily mistaken for the Spirit, even by those who have made progress, unless they continue to maintain a pure faith [Bengel]. <div eID="gen35018" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ce15536310ab8d8ef3a767d088dac338c831db4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17470"/><div sID="gen35019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17470"/><hi type="bold">4. Have ye suffered so many things--</hi>namely, persecution from Jews and from unbelieving fellow countrymen, incited by the Jews, at the time of your conversion.<div eID="gen35019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in vain--</hi>fruitlessly, needlessly, since ye might have avoided them by professing Judaism [Grotius]. Or, shall ye, by falling from grace, lose the reward promised for all your sufferings, so that they shall be "in vain" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.11">Ga 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.2">1Co 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.17-1Cor.15.19">17-19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.29-1Cor.15.32">29-32</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.5-2Thess.1.7">2Th 1:5-7</reference>; 2Jo 8)?<div eID="gen35020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet--</hi>rather, "If it be really (or 'indeed') in vain" [Ellicott]. "If, as it must be, what I have said, 'in vain,' is really the fact" [Alford]. I prefer understanding it as a mitigation of the preceding words. I hope better things of you, for I trust you will return from legalism to grace; if so, as I confidently expect, you will not have "suffered so many things in vain" [Estius]. For "God has given you the Spirit and has wrought mighty works among you" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.5">Ga 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.32-Heb.10.36">He 10:32-36</reference>) [Bengel]. <div eID="gen35021" type="x-p"/>
entries.42b65aa3355fdef167e8ab8fa6ea5edbfeff7007: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17471"/><div sID="gen35022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17471"/><hi type="bold">5. He ... that ministereth--</hi>or "supplieth," God (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.10">2Co 9:10</reference>). He who supplied and supplies to you the Spirit still, to the present time. These miracles do not prove grace to be in the heart (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.38">Mr 9:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.39">39</reference>). He speaks of these miracles as a matter of unquestioned notoriety among those addressed; an undesigned proof of their genuineness (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1-1Cor.12.31">1Co 12:1-31</reference>).<div eID="gen35022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worketh miracles among you--</hi>rather, "IN you," as <reference osisRef="Gal.2.8">Ga 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.14.2">Mt 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.13">Php 2:13</reference>; at your conversion and since [Alford].<div eID="gen35023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doeth he it by the works of the law--</hi>that is, as a consequence resulting from (so the Greek) the works of the law (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.3.2">Ga 3:2</reference>). This cannot be because the law was then unknown to you when you received those gifts of the Spirit. <div eID="gen35024" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1137f0a93a7892eb2f22b8d0e38a3b4c40b5227: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17472"/><div sID="gen35025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17472"/>6. The answer to the question in <reference osisRef="Gal.3.5">Ga 3:5</reference> is here taken for granted, It was by the hearing of faith: following this up, he says, "Even as Abraham believed," &c. (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.4-Gen.15.6">Ge 15:4-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.3">Ro 4:3</reference>). God supplies unto you the Spirit as the result of faith, not works, just as Abraham obtained justification by faith, not by works (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.6">Ga 3:6</reference>, 8, 16; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.22">Ga 4:22</reference>, 26, 28). Where justification is, there the Spirit is, so that if the former comes by faith, the latter must also. <div eID="gen35025" type="x-p"/>
entries.83dc4f7256abb16ddca6219cdf93b48ec329dd10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17473"/><div sID="gen35026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17473"/><hi type="bold">7. they which are of faith--</hi>as the source and starting-point of their spiritual life. The same phrase is in the Greek of <reference osisRef="Rom.3.26">Ro 3:26</reference>.<div eID="gen35026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same--</hi>these, and these alone, to the exclusion of all the other descendants of Abraham.<div eID="gen35027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children--</hi>Greek, "sons" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.29">Ga 3:29</reference>). <div eID="gen35028" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc98247d2c545288b133a9c0b4e0fdbd9322078b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17474"/><div sID="gen35029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17474"/><hi type="bold">8. And--</hi>Greek, "Moreover."<div eID="gen35029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foreseeing--</hi>One great excellency of Scripture is, that in it all points liable ever to be controverted, are, with prescient wisdom, decided in the most appropriate language.<div eID="gen35030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">would justify--</hi>rather, "justifieth." Present indicative. It is now, and at all times, God's one way of justification.<div eID="gen35031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the heathen--</hi>rather, "the Gentiles"; or "the nations," as the same Greek is translated at the end of the verse. God justifieth the Jews, too, "by faith, not by works." But he specifies the Gentiles in particular here, as it was their case that was in question, the Galatians being Gentiles.<div eID="gen35032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preached before the gospel--</hi>"announced beforehand the Gospel." For the "promise" was substantially the Gospel by anticipation. Compare <reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">He 4:2</reference>. A proof that "the old fathers did not look only for transitory promises" [Article VII, Church of England]. Thus the Gospel, in its essential germ, is older than the law though the full development of the former is subsequent to the latter.<div eID="gen35033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">In thee--</hi>not "in thy seed," which is a point not here raised; but strictly "in thee," as followers of thy faith, it having first shown the way to justification before God [Alford]; or "in thee," as Father of the promised seed, namely, Christ (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Ga 3:16</reference>), who is the Object of faith (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.18">Ge 22:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Psa 72:17</reference>), and imitating thy faith (see on <reference osisRef="Gal.3.9">Ga 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen35034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all nations--</hi>or as above, "all the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.18">18:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.22.18">22:18</reference>).<div eID="gen35035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be blessed--</hi>an act of grace, not something earned by works. The blessing of justification was to Abraham by faith in the promise, not by works. So to those who follow Abraham, the father of the faithful, the blessing, that is, justification, comes purely by faith in Him who is the subject of the promise. <div eID="gen35036" type="x-p"/>
entries.b57cfb2a93e3712505903d1e9e3a4464104a032a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17475"/><div sID="gen35037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17475"/><hi type="bold">9. they--</hi>and they alone.<div eID="gen35037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of faith--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Gal.3.7">Ga 3:7</reference>, beginning).<div eID="gen35038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>together with.<div eID="gen35039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faithful--</hi>implying what it is in which they are "blessed together with him," namely, faith, the prominent feature of his character, and of which the result to all who like him have it, is justification. <div eID="gen35040" type="x-p"/>
entries.a82adc506937c00221224bd8a4c52740938112bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17476"/><div sID="gen35041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17476"/>10. Confirmation of <reference osisRef="Gal.3.9">Ga 3:9</reference>. They who depend on the works of the law cannot share the blessing, for they are under the curse "written," <reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">De 27:26</reference>, Septuagint. Perfect obedience is required by the words, "in all things." Continual obedience by the word, "continueth." No man renders this obedience (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">Ro 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.20">20</reference>). It is observable, Paul quotes Scripture to the Jews who were conversant with it, as in Epistle to the Hebrews, as said or spoken; but to the Gentiles, as written. So Matthew, writing for Jews, quotes it as "said," or "spoken"; Mark and Luke, writing for Gentiles, as "written" (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.22">Mt 1:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.1.2">Mr 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.22">Lu 2:22</reference>, 23) [Townson]. <div eID="gen35041" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7ac6d2dcc79a86e624dbc33fe876e0a684cba5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17477"/><div sID="gen35042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17477"/><hi type="bold">11. by the law--</hi>Greek, "IN the law." Both in and by are included. The syllogism in this verse and <reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">Ga 3:12</reference>, is, according to Scripture, "The just shall live by faith." But the law is not of faith, but of doing, or works (that is, does not make faith, but works, the conditional ground of justifying). Therefore "in," or "by the law, no man is justified before God" (whatever the case may be before men, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.2">Ro 4:2</reference>)--not even if he could, which he cannot, keep the law, because the Scripture element and conditional mean of justification is faith.<div eID="gen35042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The just shall live by faith--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Ha 2:4</reference>). Not as Bengel and Alford, "He who is just by faith shall live." The Greek supports English Version. Also the contrast is between "live by faith" (namely, as the ground and source of his justification), and "live in them," namely, in his doings or works (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">Ga 3:12</reference>), as the conditional element wherein he is justified. <div eID="gen35043" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2c3e8861504aee43868b558437b153c4709d90b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17478"/><div sID="gen35044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17478"/><hi type="bold">12. doeth--</hi>Many depended on the law although they did not keep it; but without doing, saith Paul, it is of no use to them (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.13">Ro 2:13</reference>, 17, 23; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">10:5</reference>). <div eID="gen35044" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3364fe6973ac122d8362942ac2cde68096dd841: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17479"/><div sID="gen35045" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17479"/>13. Abrupt exclamation, as he breaks away impatiently from those who would involve us again in the curse of the law, by seeking justification in it, to "Christ," who "has redeemed us from its curse." The "us" refers primarily to the Jews, to whom the law principally appertained, in contrast to "the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Ga 3:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.4.3">Ga 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">4</reference>). But it is not restricted solely to the Jews, as Alford thinks; for these are the representative people of the world at large, and their "law" is the embodiment of what God requires of the whole world. The curse of its non-fulfilment affects the Gentiles through the Jews; for the law represents that righteousness which God requires of all, and which, since the Jews failed to fulfil, the Gentiles are equally unable to fulfil. <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">Ga 3:10</reference>, "As many as are of the works of the law, are under the curse," refers plainly, not to the Jews only, but to all, even Gentiles (as the Galatians), who seek justification by the law. The Jews' law represents the universal law which condemned the Gentiles, though with less clear consciousness on their part (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.1-Rom.2.29">Ro 2:1-29</reference>). The revelation of God's "wrath" by the law of conscience, in some degree prepared the Gentiles for appreciating redemption through Christ when revealed. The curse had to be removed from off the heathen, too, as well as the Jews, in order that the blessing, through Abraham, might flow to them. Accordingly, the "we," in "that we might receive the promise of the Spirit," plainly refers to both Jews and Gentiles.<div eID="gen35045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redeemed us--</hi>bought us off from our former bondage (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.5">Ga 4:5</reference>), and "from the curse" under which all lie who trust to the law and the works of the law for justification. The Gentile Galatians, by putting themselves under the law, were involving themselves in the curse from which Christ has redeemed the Jews primarily, and through them the Gentiles. The ransom price He paid was His own precious blood (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Mt 20:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">1Co 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.23">7:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1Ti 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1">2Pe 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Re 5:9</reference>).<div eID="gen35046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being made--</hi>Greek, "having become."<div eID="gen35047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a curse for us--</hi>Having become what we were, in our behalf, "a curse," that we might cease to be a curse. Not merely accursed (in the concrete), but a curse in the abstract, bearing the universal curse of the whole human race. So <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>, "Sin for us," not sinful, but bearing the whole sin of our race, regarded as one vast aggregate of sin. See Note there. "Anathema" means "set apart to God," to His glory, but to the person's own destruction. "Curse," an execration.<div eID="gen35048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">written--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.21.23">De 21:23</reference>). Christ's bearing the particular curse of hanging on the tree, is a sample of the "general" curse which He representatively bore. Not that the Jews put to death malefactors by hanging; but after having put them to death otherwise, in order to brand them with peculiar ignominy, they hung the bodies on a tree, and such malefactors were accursed by the law (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.5.30">Ac 5:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.39">10:39</reference>). God's providence ordered it so that to fulfil the prophecy of the curse and other prophecies, Jesus should be crucified, and so hang on the tree, though that death was not a Jewish mode of execution. The Jews accordingly, in contempt, call Him Tolvi, "the hanged one," and Christians, "worshippers of the hanged one"; and make it their great objection that He died the accursed death [Trypho, in Justin Martyr, p. 249] (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>). Hung between heaven and earth as though unworthy of either! <div eID="gen35049" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2a38b8921240ab1515bd13e7f6febc65d78c489: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17480"/><div sID="gen35050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17480"/>14. The intent of "Christ becoming a curse for us"; "To the end that upon the Gentiles the blessing of Abraham (that is, promised to Abraham, namely, justification by faith) might come in Christ Jesus" (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.3.8">Ga 3:8</reference>).<div eID="gen35050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we might receive the promise of the Spirit--</hi>the promised Spirit (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joe 2:28</reference>, 29; <reference osisRef="Luke.24.49">Lu 24:49</reference>). This clause follows not the clause immediately preceding (for our receiving the Spirit is not the result of the blessing of Abraham coming on the Gentiles), but "Christ hath redeemed us," &c.<div eID="gen35051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through faith--</hi>not by works. Here he resumes the thought in <reference osisRef="Gal.3.2">Ga 3:2</reference>. "The Spirit from without, kindles within us some spark of faith Whereby we lay hold of Christ, and even of the Spirit Himself, that He may dwell within us" [Flacius]. <div eID="gen35052" type="x-p"/>
entries.5eace8f4ea11a9472e6dc479ad27708f001725f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17481"/><div sID="gen35053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17481"/><hi type="bold">15. I speak after the manner of men--</hi>I take an illustration from a merely human transaction of everyday occurrence.<div eID="gen35053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but a man's covenant--</hi>whose purpose it is far less important to maintain.<div eID="gen35054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if it be confirmed--</hi>when once it hath been ratified.<div eID="gen35055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man disannulleth--</hi>"none setteth aside," not even the author himself, much less any second party. None does so who acts in common equity. Much less would the righteous God do so. The law is here, by personification, regarded as a second person, distinct from, and subsequent to, the promise of God. The promise is everlasting, and more peculiarly belongs to God. The law is regarded as something extraneous, afterwards introduced, exceptional and temporary (Ga 3:17-19, 21-24).<div eID="gen35056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">addeth--</hi>None addeth new conditions "making" the covenant "of none effect" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.17">Ga 3:17</reference>). So legal Judaism could make no alteration in the fundamental relation between God and man, already established by the promises to Abraham; it could not add as a new condition the observance of the law, in which case the fulfilment of the promise would be attached to a condition impossible for man to perform. The "covenant" here is one of free grace, a promise afterwards carried into effect in the Gospel. <div eID="gen35057" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb154c24dce42f752139ca7c076009f781da7437: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17482"/><div sID="gen35058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17482"/>16. This verse is parenthetical. The covenant of promise was not "spoken" (so Greek for "made") to Abraham alone, but "to Abraham and his seed"; to the latter especially; and this means Christ (and that which is inseparable from Him, the literal Israel, and the spiritual, His body, the Church). Christ not having come when the law was given, the covenant could not have been then fulfilled, but awaited the coming of Him, the Seed, to whom it was spoken.<div eID="gen35058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">promises--</hi>plural, because the same promise was often repeated (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">15:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">17:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.22.18">22:18</reference>), and because it involved many things; earthly blessings to the literal children of Abraham in Canaan, and spiritual and heavenly blessings to his spiritual children; but both promised to Christ, "the Seed" and representative Head of the literal and spiritual Israel alike. In the spiritual seed there is no distinction of Jew or Greek; but to the literal seed, the promises still in part remain to be fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>). The covenant was not made with "many" seeds (which if there had been, a pretext might exist for supposing there was one seed before the law, another under the law; and that those sprung from one seed, say the Jewish, are admitted on different terms, and with a higher degree of acceptability, than those sprung from the Gentile seed), but with the one seed; therefore, the promise that in Him "all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>), joins in this one Seed, Christ, Jew and Gentile, as fellow heirs on the same terms of acceptability, namely, by grace through faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.13">Ro 4:13</reference>); not to some by promise, to others by the law, but to all alike, circumcised and uncircumcised, constituting but one seed in Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.16">Ro 4:16</reference>). The law, on the other hand, contemplates the Jews and Gentiles as distinct seeds. God makes a covenant, but it is one of promise; whereas the law is a covenant of works. Whereas the law brings in a mediator, a third party (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.20">20</reference>), God makes His covenant of promise with the one seed, Christ (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Ge 17:7</reference>), and embraces others only as they are identified with, and represented by, Christ.<div eID="gen35059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one ... Christ--</hi>not in the exclusive sense, the man Christ Jesus, but "Christ" (Jesus is not added, which would limit the meaning), including His people who are part of Himself, the Second Adam, and Head of redeemed humanity. <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.29">29</reference> prove this, "Ye are all ONE in Christ Jesus" (Jesus is added here as the person is indicated). "And if ye be Christ's, ye are Abraham's SEED, heirs according to the promise." <div eID="gen35060" type="x-p"/>
entries.3161de788d841d2e031a4af1be52fd962679bd11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17483"/><div sID="gen35061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17483"/><hi type="bold">17. this I say--</hi>"this is what I mean," by what I said in <reference osisRef="Gal.3.15">Ga 3:15</reference>.<div eID="gen35061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continued ... of God--</hi>"ratified by God" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.15">Ga 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen35062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ--</hi>rather, "unto Christ" (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Ga 3:16</reference>). However, Vulgate and the old Italian versions translate as English Version. But the oldest manuscripts omit the words altogether.<div eID="gen35063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the law which was--</hi>Greek, "which came into existence four hundred thirty years after" (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.40">Ex 12:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">41</reference>). He does not, as in the case of "the covenant," add "enacted by God" (<reference osisRef="John.1.17">Joh 1:17</reference>). The dispensation of "the promise" began with the call of Abraham from Ur into Canaan, and ended on the last night of his grandson Jacob's sojourn in Canaan, the land of promise. The dispensation of the law, which engenders bondage, was beginning to draw on from the time of his entrance into Egypt, the land of bondage. It was to Christ in him, as in his grandfather Abraham, and his father Isaac, not to him or them as persons, the promise was spoken. On the day following the last repetition of the promise orally (<reference osisRef="Gen.46.1-Gen.46.6">Ge 46:1-6</reference>), at Beer-sheba, Israel passed into Egypt. It is from the end, not from the beginning of the dispensation of promise, that the interval of four hundred thirty years between it and the law is to be counted. At Beer-sheba, after the covenant with Abimelech, Abraham called on the everlasting God, and the well was confirmed to him and his seed as an everlasting possession. Here God appeared to Isaac. Here Jacob received the promise of the blessing, for which God had called Abraham out of Ur, repeated for the last time, on the last night of his sojourn in the land of promise.<div eID="gen35064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot--</hi>Greek, "doth not disannul."<div eID="gen35065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make ... of none effect--</hi>The promise would become so, if the power of conferring the inheritance be transferred from it to the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.14">Ro 4:14</reference>). <div eID="gen35066" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd23ca3c46c3bed4dc5238566d51895ccee82a12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17484"/><div sID="gen35067" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17484"/><hi type="bold">18. the inheritance--</hi>all the blessings to be inherited by Abraham's literal and spiritual children, according to the promise made to him and to his Seed, Christ, justification and glorification (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.7">Ga 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Ro 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.9">1Co 6:9</reference>).<div eID="gen35067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but God, &c.--</hi>The Greek order requires rather, "But to Abraham it was by promise that God hath given it." The conclusion is, Therefore the inheritance is not of, or from the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.14">Ro 4:14</reference>). <div eID="gen35068" type="x-p"/>
entries.f93508d3170d72719160d679444abea1c0744814: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17485"/><div sID="gen35069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17485"/>19. "Wherefore then serveth the law?" as it is of no avail for justification, is it either useless, or contrary to the covenant of God? [Calvin].<div eID="gen35069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">added--</hi>to the original covenant of promise. This is not inconsistent with <reference osisRef="Gal.3.15">Ga 3:15</reference>, "No man addeth thereto"; for there the kind of addition meant, and therefore denied, is one that would add new conditions, inconsistent with the grace of the covenant of promise. The law, though misunderstood by the Judaizers as doing so, was really added for a different purpose, namely, "because of (or as the Greek, 'for the sake of') the transgressions," that is, to bring out into clearer view the transgressions of it (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.7-Rom.7.9">Ro 7:7-9</reference>); to make men more fully conscious of their "sins," by being perceived as transgressions of the law, and so to make them long for the promised Saviour. This accords with <reference osisRef="Gal.3.23">Ga 3:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.15">Ro 4:15</reference>. The meaning can hardly be "to check transgressions," for the law rather stimulates the corrupt heart to disobey it (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Ro 5:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.13">7:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till the seed--</hi>during the period up to the time when the seed came. The law was a preparatory dispensation for the Jewish nation (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Ro 5:20</reference>; Greek, "the law came in additionally and incidentally"), intervening between the promise and its fulfilment in Christ.<div eID="gen35071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come--</hi>(Compare "faith came," <reference osisRef="Gal.3.23">Ga 3:23</reference>).<div eID="gen35072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the promise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.4.21">Ro 4:21</reference>).<div eID="gen35073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ordained--</hi>Greek, "constituted" or "disposed."<div eID="gen35074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by angels--</hi>as the instrumental enactors of the law [Alford] God delegated the law to angels as something rather alien to Him and severe (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.53">Ac 7:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.2">He 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">De 33:2</reference>, "He came with ten thousands of saints," that is, angels, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>). He reserved "the promise" to Himself and dispensed it according to His own goodness.<div eID="gen35075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the hand of a mediator--</hi>namely, Moses. <reference osisRef="Deut.5.5">De 5:5</reference>, "I stood between the Lord and you": the very definition of a mediator. Hence the phrase often recurs, "By the hand of Moses." In the giving of the law, the "angels" were representatives of God; Moses, as mediator, represented the people. <div eID="gen35076" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7b81018f717b735f2611081282138c7749bfb5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17486"/><div sID="gen35077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17486"/><hi type="bold">20. "Now a mediator cannot be of one (but must be of two parties whom he mediates between); but God is one" (not two: owing to His essential unity not admitting of an intervening party between Him and those to be blessed; but as the One Sovereign, His own representative, giving the blessing directly by promise to Abraham, and, in its fulfilment, to Christ, "the Seed," without new condition, and without a mediator such as the law had). The conclusion understood is, Therefore a mediator cannot appertain to God; and consequently, the law, with its inseparable appendage of a mediator, cannot be the normal way of dealing of God, the one, and unchangeable God, who dealt with Abraham by direct promise, as a sovereign, not as one forming a compact with another party, with conditions and a mediator attached thereto. God would bring man into immediate communion with Him, and not have man separated from Him by a mediator that keeps back from access, as Moses and the legal priesthood did (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.12">Ex 19:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.17">13, 17</reference>, 21-24; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.19-Heb.12.24">He 12:19-24</reference>). The law that thus interposed a mediator and conditions between man and God, was an exceptional state limited to the Jews, and parenthetically preparatory to the Gospel, God's normal mode of dealing, as He dealt with Abraham, namely, face to face directly; by promise and grace, and not conditions; to all nations united by faith in the one seed (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>, 16, 18), and not to one people to the exclusion and severance from the One common Father, of all other nations. It is no objection to this view, that the Gospel, too, has a mediator (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>).
