Dreading no farther contradiction, now that the point is settled, Paul concludes, that the former arguments have placed it beyond a doubt, and exclaims: “Who will now dare to imagine a disagreement between the law and the promises?” And yet this does not prevent Paul from proceeding to remove the difficulties that might still arise.<div eID="gen123809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123810" type="x-p"/>Before answering the question, he expresses, in his usual manner, a high disdain of such folly; thus intimating the strong abhorrence with which pious men must regard whatever brings reproach on the Divine character. But another instance of high address, which claims our notice, is found in this turn of expression. He charges his adversaries with the offense of making God contradict himself. For from him the Law and the promises have evidently proceeded: whoever then alleges any contradiction between them blasphemes against God: but they do contradict each other, if the Law justifies. Thus does Paul most dexterously retort upon his adversaries the charge which they falsely and calumniously brought against him.<div eID="gen123810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123811" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For if there had been a law given</hi>. The reply is (what is called) indirect, and does not plainly assert an agreement between the law and the promises, but contains all that is necessary to remove the contradiction. At first sight, you would say that this sentence departs from the context, and has nothing to do with the solution of the question; but this is not the case. The law would be opposed to the promises, if it had the power of justifying; for there would be two opposite methods of justifying a man, two separate roads towards the attainment of righteousness. But Paul refuses to the law such a power; so that the contradiction is removed. I would admit, says he, that righteousness is obtained by the law, if salvation were found in it. But what?<div eID="gen123811" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen123808" osisID="Gal.3.21" type="section"/>
entries.78158d2cdd647747a94e2408a378dbc2c958f270:
22. The Scripture hath concluded. By the word Scripture is chiefly intended the law itself. It “hath concluded all under sin,” and therefore, instead of giving, it takes away righteousness from all. The reasoning is most powerful. “You seek righteousness in the law: but the law itself, with the whole of Scripture, leaves nothing to men but condemnation; for all men, with their works, are pronounced to be unrighteous: who then shall live by the law?” He alludes to these words,
“He who shall do these things, shall live in them.” (Leviticus 18:5.)
Shut out by it, says he, from life through guilt, in vain should we seek salvation by the law. — The word translated all (τὰ πάντα) signifies all things, and conveys more than if he had said all men; for it embraces not only men, but every thing which they possess or can accomplish.
That the promise by faith. There is no remedy but to throw away the righteousness of works, and betake ourselves to the faith of Christ. The result is certain. If works come into judgment, we are all condemned; therefore we obtain, by the faith of Christ, a free righteousness. This sentence is full of the highest consolation. It tells us that, wherever we hear ourselves condemned in Scripture, there is help provided for us in Christ, if we betake ourselves to him. We are lost, though God were silent: why then does he so often pronounce that we are lost? It is that we may not perish by everlasting destruction, but, struck and confounded by such a dreadful sentence, may by faith seek Christ, through whom we “pass from death into life.” (1 John 3:14.) By a figure of speech, (μετωνυμία,) in which the thing containing is put for the thing contained, the promise denotes that which is promised.
Galatians 3:23-29
23. But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed.
23. Antequam autem veniret fides, sub Lege custodiebamur, conclusi sub fidem, quae revelanda erat.
24. Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
24. Itaque Lex paedagogus noster fuit in Christum, ut ex fide justificaremur.
25. But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.
25. Adveniente autem fide, non amplius sub paedagogo sumus.
26. For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus.
26. Nam omnes filii Dei estis per fidem in Christo Iesu.
27. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
27. Siquidem quicunque in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis.
28. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
28. Non est Iudaeus neque Graecus, non est servus neque liber, non est masculus neque femina; onmes enim vos unus estis in Christo Iesu.
29. And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.
29. Si autem vos Christi, ergo semen Abrahae estis, et secundum promissionem haeredes.
entries.bcbcf5e8108979463314fd30366e99b9b40dc8ca: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.3.23" sID="gen123834" type="section"/> <div sID="gen123835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> <hi type="italic">Before faith came</hi>. The question proposed is now more fully defined. He explains at great length the use of the law, and the reason why it was temporal; for otherwise it would have appeared to be always unreasonable that a law should be delivered to the Jews, from which the Gentiles were excluded. If there be but one church consisting of Jews and Gentiles, why is there a diversity in its government? Whence is this new liberty derived, and on what authority does it rest, since the fathers were under subjection to the law? He therefore informs us, that the distinction is such as not to interrupt the union and harmony of the church.<div eID="gen123835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123836" type="x-p"/>We must again remind the reader that Paul does not treat exclusively of ceremonies, or of the moral law, but embraces the whole economy by which the Lord governed his people under the Old Testament. It became a subject of dispute whether the form of government instituted by Moses had any influence in obtaining righteousness. Paul compares this law first to a <hi type="italic">prison</hi>, and next to a <hi type="italic">schoolmaster</hi>. Such was the nature of the law, as both comparisons plainly show, that it could not have been in force beyond a certain time.<div eID="gen123836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123837" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Faith</hi> denotes the full revelation of those things which, during the darkness of the shadows of the law, were dimly seen; for he does not intend to say that the fathers, who lived under the law, did not possess faith. The faith of Abraham has already come under our notice, and other instances are quoted by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.11">Hebrews 11</reference>.) The doctrine of faith, in short, is attested by Moses and all the prophets: but, as faith was not then clearly manifested, so the <hi type="italic">time of faith</hi> is an appellation here given, not in an absolute, but in a comparative sense, to the time of the New Testament. That this was his meaning is evident from what he immediately adds, that they were <hi type="italic">shut up under the faith which should afterwards be revealed;</hi> for this implies that those who were under the custody of the law were partakers of the same faith. The law did not restrain them from faith; but, that they might not wander from the fold of faith, it kept possession of themselves. There is an elegant allusion, too, to what he had formerly said, that “the scripture hath concluded all under sin.” They were besieged on every hand by the curse, but this siege was counteracted by an imprisonment which protected them from the curse; so that the imprisonment by the law is here proved to have been highly generous in its character.<div eID="gen123837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123838" type="x-p"/>Faith was not yet<hi type="italic"> revealed</hi>, not because the fathers wanted light, but because they had less light than we have. The ceremonies might be said to shadow out an absent Christ, but to us he is represented as actually present, and thus while they had the mirror, we have the substance. Whatever might be the amount of darkness under the law, the fathers were not ignorant of the road in which they ought to walk. Though the dawn is not equal to the splendor of noon, yet, as it is sufficient to direct a journey, travelers do not wait till the sun is fully risen. Their portion of light resembled the dawn, which was enough to preserve them from all error, and guide them to everlasting blessedness.<div eID="gen123838" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen123834" osisID="Gal.3.23" type="section"/>
entries.717bbb08c7e5e4549ab0b33a9d530cefa8db6588:
24. Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster This is the second comparison, which still more clearly expresses Paul’s design. A schoolmaster is not appointed for the whole life, but only for childhood, as the etymology of the Greek word παιδαγωγός implies.
“As the law was before compared to a jailer, so it is here likened to a παιδαγωγός, by which term is not to be understood a schoolmaster, (for that would have been διδάσκαλος,) but the paedagous or person (usually a freedman or slave) who conducted children to and from school, attended them out of school hours, formed their manners, superintended their moral conduct, and in various respects prepared them for the διδάσκαλος.” — Bloomfield. Our author’s observations on παιδαγωγός, in another passage, have brought out the full meaning of this word, and the classical authorities for the use of it, in the translator’s notes. — Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 1, p. 169. — Ed
Besides, in training a child, the object is to prepare him, by the instructions of childhood, for maturer years. The comparison applies in both respects to the law, for its authority was limited to a particular age, and its whole object was to prepare its scholars in such a manner, that, when its elementary instructions were closed, they might make progress worthy of manhood. And so he adds, that it was our schoolmaster (εἰς Χριστὸν) unto Christ. The grammarian, when he has trained a boy, delivers him into the hands of another, who conducts him through the higher branches of a finished education. In like manner, the law was the grammar of theology, which, after carrying its scholars a short way, handed them over to faith to be completed. Thus, Paul compares the Jews to children, and us to advanced youth.
But a question arises, what was the instruction or education of this schoolmaster? First, the law, by displaying the justice of God, convinced them that in themselves they were unrighteous; for in the commandments of God, as in a mirror, they might see how far they were distant from true righteousness. They were thus reminded that righteousness must be sought in some other quarter. The promises of the law served the same purpose, and might lead to such reflections as these: “If you cannot obtain life by works but by fulfilling the law, some new and different method must be sought. Your weakness will never allow you to ascend so high; nay, though you desire and strive ever so much, you will fall far short of the object.” The threatenings, on the other hand, pressed and entreated them to seek refuge from the wrath and curse of God, and gave them no rest till they were constrained to seek the grace of Christ.
Such too, was the tendency of all the ceremonies; for what end did sacrifices and washings serve but to keep the mind continually fixed on pollution and condemnation? When a man’s uncleanness is placed before his eyes, when the unoffending animal is held forth as the image of his own death, how can he indulge in sleep? How can he but be roused to the earnest cry for deliverance? Beyond all doubt, ceremonies accomplished their object, not merely by alarming and humbling the conscience, but by exciting them to the faith of the coming Redeemer. In the imposing services of the Mosaic ritual, every thing that was presented to the eye bore an impress of Christ. The law, in short, was nothing else than an immense variety of exercises, in which the worshippers were led by the hand to Christ.
That we might be justified by faith. He has already said that the law is not perfect, when he compared it to the training of childhood; but it would make men perfect if it bestowed upon them righteousness. What remains but that faith shall take its place? And so it does, when we, who are destitute of a righteousness of our own, are clothed by it with the righteousness of Christ. Thus is the saying accomplished, “he hath filled the hungry with good things.” (Luke 1:53.)
entries.7fb3b173c844a9764ad444333abad389cd6eb45b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.3.25" sID="gen123845" type="section"/> <div sID="gen123846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">But after that faith is come</hi>. This phrase has been already considered. It denotes the brighter revelation of grace after that “the vail of the temple was rent in twain,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.51">Matthew 27:51</reference>,) which, we know, was effected by the manifestation of Christ. He affirms that, under the reign of Christ, there is no longer any childhood which needs to be placed under a schoolmaster, and that, consequently, the law has resigned its office, — which is another application of the comparison. There were two things which he had undertaken to prove, — that the law is a preparation for Christ, and that it is temporal. But here the question is again put, Is the law so abolished that we have nothing to do with it? I answer, the law, so far as it is a rule of life, a bridle to keep us in the fear of the Lord, a spur to correct the sluggishness of our flesh, — so far, in short, as it is<div eID="gen123846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123847" type="x-p"/>“profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that believers may be instructed in every good work,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Tim.3.16 Bible:2Tim.3.17">2 Timothy 3:16, 17</reference>,)<div eID="gen123847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123848" type="x-p"/>— is as much in force as ever, and remains untouched.<div eID="gen123848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123849" type="x-p"/>In what respect, then, is it abolished? Paul, we have said, looks at the law as possessing certain qualities, and those qualities we shall enumerate. It annexes to works a reward and a punishment; that is, it promises life to those who keep it, and curses all transgressors. Meanwhile, it requires from man the highest perfection and most exact obedience. It makes no abatement, gives no pardon, but calls to a severe reckoning the smallest offenses. It does not openly exhibit Christ and his grace, but points him out at a distance, and only when hidden by the covering of ceremonies. All such qualities of the law, Paul tells us, are abolished; so that the office of Moses is now at an end, so far as it differs in outward aspect from a covenant of grace.<div eID="gen123849" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen123845" osisID="Gal.3.25" type="section"/>
entries.505214686c18d385b7b303f3aa8e772c584f4a45: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.3.26" sID="gen123850" type="section"/> <div sID="gen123851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">For ye are all the children of God</hi>. It would be unjust, and in the highest degree unreasonable, that the law should hold believers in perpetual slavery. This is proved by the additional argument, that they are the children of God. It would not be enough to say that we are no longer children, unless it were added that we are freemen; for in slaves age makes no alteration. The fact of their being the children of God proves their freedom. How? <hi type="italic">By faith in Christ Jesus;</hi> for<div eID="gen123851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123852" type="x-p"/>“as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.12">John 1:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen123852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123853" type="x-p"/>Since, then, by faith we have obtained adoption, by faith likewise we have obtained our freedom.<div eID="gen123853" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen123850" osisID="Gal.3.26" type="section"/>
entries.aa597216cd8435a8daf14366c76a11089175cfe8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.3.27" sID="gen123854" type="section"/> <div sID="gen123855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> <hi type="italic">As many of you as have been baptized</hi>. The greater and loftier the privilege is of being the children of God, the farther is it removed from our senses, and the more difficult to obtain belief. He therefore explains, in a few words, what is implied in our being united, or rather, made one with the Son of God; so as to remove all doubt, that what belongs to him is communicated to us. He employs the metaphor of a garment, when he says that the Galatians <hi type="italic">have put on Christ</hi>; but he means that they are so closely united to him, that, in the presence of God, they bear the name and character of Christ, and are viewed in him rather than in themselves. This metaphor or similitude, taken from garments, occurs frequently, and has been treated by us in other places.<div eID="gen123855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123856" type="x-p"/>But the argument, that, because they have been baptized, they have put on Christ, appears weak; for how far is baptism from being efficacious in all? Is it reasonable that the grace of the Holy Spirit should be so closely linked to an external symbol? Does not the uniform doctrine of Scripture, as well as experience, appear to confute this statement? I answer, it is customary with Paul to treat of the sacraments in two points of view. When he is dealing with hypocrites, in whom the mere symbol awakens pride, he then proclaims loudly the emptiness and worthlessness of the outward symbol, and denounces, in strong terms, their foolish confidence. In such cases he contemplates not the ordinance of God, but the corruption of wicked men. When, on the other hand, he addresses believers, who make a proper use of the symbols, he then views them in connection with the truth — which they represent. In this case, he makes no boast of any false splendor as belonging to the sacraments, but calls our attention to the actual fact represented by the outward ceremony. Thus, agreeably to the Divine appointment, the truth comes to be associated with the symbols.<div eID="gen123856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123857" type="x-p"/>But perhaps some person will ask, Is it then possible that, through the fault of men, a sacrament shall cease to bear a figurative meaning? The reply is easy. Though wicked men may derive no advantage from the sacraments, they still retain undiminished their nature and force. The sacraments present, both to good and to bad men, the grace of God. No falsehood attaches to the promises which they exhibit of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Believers receive what is offered; and if wicked men, by rejecting it, render the offer unprofitable to themselves, their conduct cannot destroy the faithfulness of God, or the true meaning of the sacrament. <note n="64"> <div sID="gen123858" type="x-p"/> “If any person receives nothing more than this bodily washing, which is perceived by the eyes of flesh, he has not put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” — Jerome.<div eID="gen123858" type="x-p"/> </note> With strict propriety, then, does Paul, in addressing believers, say, that when they were baptized, they “put on Christ;” just as, in the Epistle to the Romans, he says,<div eID="gen123857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123859" type="x-p"/>“that we have been planted together into his death,<lb/> so as to be also partakers of his resurrection.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.5">Romans 6:5</reference>.)<div eID="gen123859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen123860" type="x-p"/>In this way, the symbol and the Divine operation are kept distinct, and yet the meaning of the sacraments is manifest; so that they cannot be regarded as empty and trivial exhibitions; and we are reminded with what base ingratitude they are chargeable, who, by abusing the precious ordinances of God, not only render them unprofitable to themselves, but turn them to their own destruction!<div eID="gen123860" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen123854" osisID="Gal.3.27" type="section"/>
entries.5fb25507d41bb31ccfac324454de2d7b4ad740a9: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gal.3.28" sID="gen123861" type="section"/> <div sID="gen123862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> <hi type="italic">There is neither Jew nor Greek</hi>. The meaning is, that there is no distinction of persons here, and therefore it is of no consequence to what nation or condition any one may belong: nor is circumcision any more regarded than sex or civil rank. And why? Because Christ makes them all one. Whatever may have been their former differences, Christ alone is able to unite them all. <hi type="italic">Ye are one:</hi> the distinction is now removed. The apostle’s object is to shew that the grace of adoption, and the hope of salvation, do not depend on the law, but are contained in Christ alone, who therefore is all. Greek is here put, as usual, for Gentile, and one department for the whole class.<div eID="gen123862" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gal.3.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen123861" osisID="Gal.3.28" type="section"/>
entries.f746a33e6b4057828a78d7bd7a88a0e8c14634d0:
29. Then are ye Abraham’s seed. This is not intended to convey the idea, that to be a child of Abraham is better than to be a member of Christ, — but to repress the pride of the Jews, who gloried in their privilege, as if they alone were the people of God. They reckoned no distinction higher than to belong to the race of Abraham; and this very distinction he makes to be common to all who believe in Christ. The conclusion rests on this argument, that Christ is the blessed seed, in whom, as we have said, all the children of Abraham are united. He proves this by the universal offer of the inheritance to them all, from which it follows, that the promise includes them among the children. It deserves notice, that, wherever faith is mentioned, it is always his relation to the promise.
CHAPTER 4
Galatians 4:1-5
1. Now I say, That the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all;
1. Dico antem: quamdiu haeres puer est, nihil differt a servo, quum tamen sit dominus onmium;
2. But is under tutors and governors, until the time appointed of the father.
2. Sed sub tutoribus et curatorbus est, usque ad tempus a patre definitum.
3. Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world:
3. Sic et nos quum essemus pueri, sub elementis mundi in servitute eramus.
4. But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,
4. Quando autem venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum, facturn ex muliere, redactum sub Legem;
5. To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.
5. Ut eos, qui sub Lege erant, redimeter, ut adoptionem reciperemus.

entries.e340c0e27141c37425544a577d04555a7f8f687b:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="3" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. III.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 O Foolish Galatians, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 5.7.</ns0:note> who hath bewitched you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle beginnet<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the further pursuit of the argument he was upon, with a smart reprehension of them; as men of no understanding, and <ns0:hi>bewitched.</ns0:hi> The word translated <ns0:hi>bewitched</ns0:hi> signifies vitiating the eyes, or spoiling the sight, so as that men cannot discern an obvious object in a due position. The mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing is, who hath seduced you, who hath so corrupted your un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstanding that your actings are as inaccountable, as the ef<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fects of witchcraft?</ns0:note>, that you should not obey the truth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The word translated <ns0:hi>obey,</ns0:hi> signifies also to <ns0:hi>believe,</ns0:hi> In general it signifies to be <ns0:hi>perswaded</ns0:hi>; which may refer either to an assent to the truth, or obedience to the precepts of the Gospel.</ns0:note>, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">When as Christ hath been plainly preached before you, and his Death, with the blessed end, and effects of it, hath been so made known amongst you, as if you had seen him crucified. Or else Christ may be said to be <ns0:hi>cru cified amongst them,</ns0:hi> because it was in their time, so as they could not but hear of it, and there was no more reason for them to doubt of the truth of the thing, then if he had, been crucified in their Country.</ns0:note>, crucified among you <ns0:hi>d.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 This only would I learn of you, Received ye <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 2.38. & 8.15. & 15.8. Eph. 1.13.</ns0:note> the spirit <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> here is understood the <ns0:hi>gifts of the Spirit,</ns0:hi> which were either such as were common to all believers, (such as <ns0:hi>Faith, Love,</ns0:hi> &c.) or else such as were peculiar to some, and those not all Believers; such were those abilities for miracu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lous operations given to some. Some understand this Text of the former, some of the latter; It's best to take in both; all the manifestations of the Spirit then given out, either for the Sanctification and Eternal Salvation of those to whom they were given, or for the confirmation of the Truth of the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel.</ns0:note>, by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Did you <ns0:hi>receive the Spirit by the works of the Law,</ns0:hi> that he knew they could not say they did; for they were Heathens; strangers to the Commonwealth of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> so as they could pretend to no works of the Law: Did you receive this Holy Spirit upon hearing the Gospel, (which is the Doctrine of Faith) preached to you: Men should take heed of villifying that Ministry, or that Doctrine, which God hath blessed to the change of their own hearts, or the hearts of others: We also may observe from hence, That the hearing the Gospel faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully preached is a blessed means by which mens hearts are changed, and they receive the Holy Spirit: not inabling them, (as it did some and but some in the beginning of the Gospel,) to work signs and wonders, but inabling them to the operations of a Spiritual Life: The strength of the Apostles argument is this, you have the greatest reason to own that Doctrine as the truth which God hath blessed to your Souls to produce Spiritual Effects there.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Doctrine of their false Teachers was, that to Faith in Christ, an obedience also to the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> was necessary to justification; they did not deny Christ, or the Doctrine of the Gospel, only they pleade for the works of the Law as ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary to be superadded. The Apostle calls this first owning of Christ, and imbracing the Doctrine of Faith, <ns0:hi>a beginning in the Spirit</ns0:hi>; their adding the necessity of obedience to the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>being made perfect in the flesh.</ns0:hi> And argueth the un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reasonableness of it, that their <ns0:hi>Iustification</ns0:hi> should be begun by a more noble, and made perfect by a more ignoble cause. He calls the Doctrine of the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> because (as he said in the former verse) they had received the Holy Spirit, by the <ns0:hi>hearing of faith</ns0:hi>; that is by hearing and receiving the Gospel. The works of the Law he calls <ns0:hi>flesh,</ns0:hi> because the Ordinances of the Law were (as the Apostle calls them, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.10.) <ns0:hi>Carnal Ordinances imposed on the Iews till the time of reformation.</ns0:hi> He elsewhere calls them the <ns0:hi>rudiments of the World, Col.</ns0:hi> 2.8.20. and in this Epistle, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 4.9. he calls them <ns0:hi>beggerly Elements.</ns0:hi> For though the Ordinances of the Law were in their season spiritual, they being commanded by God; yet they being but temporary constitutions, never intended by God to conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nue longer than the coming of Christ, and the Law being but a Schoolmaster to lead to Christ; Christ being now come, and having dyed, and rose again from the Dead, they became use<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less. Besides that God never intended them as other than <ns0:hi>Rudiments</ns0:hi> and first <ns0:hi>Elements,</ns0:hi> the end of which was Christ; and the observance of which without Faith in Christ, was <ns0:hi>weak</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>impotent,</ns0:hi> as to the noble end of Justification; It spake great weakness therefore in the <ns0:hi>Galatians,</ns0:hi> to begin with what was more perfect, (the embracing of the Gospel, and Christ there exhibited for the justification of sinners) and to end in what was more imperfect, thinking by that to be made per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect; or else the Apostle here chargeth them with a defection from Christ, as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 4.9, 10, 11. and <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5.4. and so calleth them foolish, for <ns0:hi>beginning in the Spirit,</ns0:hi> (the Holy Spirit in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wardly working in them the change of their hearts, and rege<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nerating them;) and then apostatizing from their profes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion to a carnal Life: But I had rather interpret <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> in this Text, of the <ns0:hi>Doctrine of the Gospel,</ns0:hi> dictated by the Spirit; and with the receiving of which, the Holy Spirit was given. And, so their folly is argued from their thinking to be made per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect by the <ns0:hi>beggerly elements,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>worldly rudiments</ns0:hi> of the Law, when as they had first begun their profession of Christianity with embracing the more perfect Doctrine of the Gospel.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:478" />4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Joh. 8.</ns0:note> H ave ye suffered so <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>so great.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> many things in vain <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">There is no doubt, but these Churches in the Regions of <ns0:hi>Galatia,</ns0:hi> had their share in the sufferings of Christians by the Jews, for their adherence to, and profession of the Doctrine of the Gospel, which they might either wholly, or in a great measure have avoided, would they have complyed with the Jews in the observance of those legal rites. Therefore, (saith the Apostle) to what purpose have you suffered so much for the owning of the Christian Religion, if you now bring your selves under the bondage of Circumcision, and other legal observances?</ns0:note>? if it be yet in vain <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">If <ns0:hi>it be in vain,</ns0:hi> by which words he either cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />recteth himself, as if he had said, but I hope better things of you, that I shall find that you did not suffer them in vain; or else he hinteth that their suffering so much would not be in vain, because by their apostacy from the true faith for which they suffered, they would in effect deny it, as if it had been false, and their former suffering would rise up in Judgment against them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 He therefore that ministreth to you the spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit, and worketh miracles among you <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Ver.</ns0:hi> 2. He had asked them, whether they had received the Spirit by the works of the Law, or by hearing the Gospel? Some think what he saith here to be a continuation of the same argument, but it rather seems a new one. There he spake of their receiving the Spirit, here he speaks of the Ministration of the Spirit: some understand it of God, who gives his Holy Spirit to them that ask him, and who was the Author of those miraculous operations wrought by the Spirit. I should rather understand it of the Ministers of the Gospel, to whom God hath committed the ministration of the Spirit; and to some of whom God in the Primitive times gave a power to work miracles.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>doth he it</ns0:hi> by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Doth God concur with our Ministry upon our preaching the Law, or upon our preaching the Gospel? So that though there be a great cognation betwixt the Apostles ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guing, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 2. and his arguing in this verse, yet there is some difference; the Apostle there arguing from the success of preaching the Gospel, here from the ministration it self.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Even as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 15.6. Rom. 4.3. Jam. 2.23.</ns0:note> Abraham believed God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">As <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was justified, so must all the children of <ns0:hi>Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham</ns0:hi>; but <ns0:hi>Abraham believed God,</ns0:hi> (that is, agreed to the truth of all those promises which God gave him, and trusted in God for the fulfilling of them; for both those acts of the mind are included in believing God<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>) and so was justified alone.</ns0:note>, and it was <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>imputed.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> accounted to him for righteousness <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">His Faith it self was not imputed to him; those that put this sense upon the words, either forget that faith it self is a work; or that the Apostle here is arguing for justification by Faith in op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />position to justification by works, and cannot be imagined to have gone about to prove that justification is not by works, by proving that it is by a work. The meaning is no more than that he was upon it accounted righteous; not that God so honoured the work of Faith, but that he so rewarded it, as being the condition annexed to the promise of justification. His faith was not his righteousness, but God so rewarded his exercise of Faith, as that upon it he reckoned (or imputed) that to him which was his righteousness, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the righteousness of him in whom he believed as revealed unto him in the promise.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Know ye therefore that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 4.12, 16.</ns0:note> they which are of faith <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Those who are Believers, and receive Jesus Christ, as exhi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bited and tendred to them in the Gospel, trusting not to any Righteousness of their own arising from their Obedience to the works of the Law:</ns0:note>, the same are the children of Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">They are the <ns0:hi>children of Abraham,</ns0:hi> conside<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red <ns0:hi>as the Father of the faithful,</ns0:hi> that is, they are justified as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was justified; who was justified not by his Circumci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion, but upon his believing in Christ exhibited to him in the promise; not by <ns0:hi>working,</ns0:hi> but by <ns0:hi>imputation.</ns0:hi> This argument came very close to the Jews, whose great glorying was in ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> to their Father; for it is in effect a saying, that they were no true children of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> none of that seed to whom the promise was made, if they expected Justification from the works of the Law, which <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> never had nor ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pected.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And the Scripture <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The Holy Ghost in Scripture, (by whose inspiration the Scripture was written) foreseeing, or knowing the Councels and designs of God, that the Heathen, (when the fulness of times as to them should come,) should be justified through Faith in Christ; preached the same Doctrine before unto <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> so as it is no new Doctrine; the Gospel which we now preach unto you, was long since revealed unto <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>; who saw Christ's day, and rejoiced. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.56.</ns0:note> foreseeing that God would justifie the heathen through faith preached before the gospel <ns0:hi>r</ns0:hi> unto Abraham, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 12.3<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 18.18. & <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 18. Act. 3.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> In thee shall all nations be blessed <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To prove which, he quoteth the promise, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 12.3. where God tells <ns0:hi>Abraham, That i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> him all the Nations of the Earth should be blessed</ns0:hi>; which quotation of it by the Apostle in this place informeth us, that it is to be understood of those Spiritual Blessings which are in Christ Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sus. For all the Nations of the Earth were no otherwise bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed in <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> then as Christ, (who is called the <ns0:hi>desire of all Nations,</ns0:hi> and he in <ns0:hi>whom the Gentiles</ns0:hi> should trust, and a <ns0:hi>light to enlighten the Gentiles,</ns0:hi>) descended from <ns0:hi>Abraham.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 So then they which be of faith <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Those that believe in Jesus Christ with such a Faith as the Gospel doth require, they, and they alone,</ns0:note>, are blessed with faithful Abraham <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">are blessed with spiritual blessings, justified from the guilt of sin; <ns0:hi>with Abraham,</ns0:hi> that is, in the same manner, that <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> the Father of the faithful, and who himself was a believer, was justified; which was not, (as was before said,) by his circumcision, or by any works that he did, but by imputation upon his believing in the Lord Jesus Christ, exhibited, and held forth in the promise made to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse, for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">To be <ns0:hi>under the Law,</ns0:hi> is under the Covenant of works, or un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the expectation of Life and Salvation only from obedience to the works of the Law. These (he saith) are under <ns0:hi>the curse,</ns0:hi> the reason of which the Apostle gives us, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.3. <ns0:hi>Because it is made weak through our flesh,</ns0:hi> could man perfectly fulfil the Law, he might expect life from it, and salvation from his obe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dience to it; but the Law curseth him <ns0:hi>that continueth not in all that is written in it; If a man keepeth the whole Law, if he offends but in one point, he is guilty of all</ns0:hi>; and as liable to the wrath of God, as if he had broken it in many things<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Hence it necessarily followeth, if no man can keep the Law of God perfectly, that all under the Law must be under the curse, and consequently cannot be blessed in faithful <ns0:hi>Abraham.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Argument is this, Those that are under a curse, cannot be under the blessing of Justification. But those that are un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the Law are under the curse. This he proves out of the Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 27.26. where those are pronounced <ns0:hi>Cursed,</ns0:hi> who <ns0:hi>continue not in all things written in the book of the Law to do them.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">

                     </ns0:gap>. 2.16.</ns0:note> that no man by the law is justified in the sight of God, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> evident <ns0:note place="margin">

                     </ns0:gap>. 38.</ns0:note>, for the just shall live by faith <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Apostle by another Argument proveth that sinners are not justified by works. He grants, they may be justified by their good and blameless living <ns0:hi>before men,</ns0:hi> so as that they may have nothing to say against them, but he says they cannot by such works be justified <ns0:hi>in the sight of God.</ns0:hi> His Argument is from the opposition that is between <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>works.</ns0:hi> He pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veth from <ns0:hi>Hab.</ns0:hi> 2.4. That we are <ns0:hi>justified by Faith</ns0:hi>: Where the Prophet saith, that the just (or righteous man) shall live by Faith, fetch his life from Faith, live his Spiritual life by Faith, and obtain Eternal life by Faith, the life of his righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness shall be by faith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And <ns0:note place="margin">

                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> the law is not of faith <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Law saith nothing of Faith in the <ns0:hi>Mediator,</ns0:hi> though faith <ns0:hi>in God</ns0:hi> be commanded in the first precept; yet Faith in Christ is not commanded by the Law as that by which the Soul shall live.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note place="margin">

                     </ns0:gap>.5.</ns0:note> the man that doth them, shall live in them <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">For that which the Law saith is, <ns0:hi>do this and live.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The man that doth the things contained in the Law, shall live in them; Life in the Law is promised to those who do the things which it requireth; not to them, who having failed in their performances, yet accept of the Lord Jesus Christ as the Redeemer which God hath sent, and believe in him who justifieth the ungodly. For that by the <ns0:hi>Life</ns0:hi> promised to the observation of the Law, not a temporal Life only is to be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood, but Eternal Life also, is plain from our Saviours ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plication of it to the young man, inquiring about the way to Eternal Life, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19.16, 17. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 10.28.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 8.3. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 5.21.</ns0:note> Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">If the Law curseth <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>all those who continue not in all things contained in the Law, (as the Apostle had said, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 10. and proved from <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 27.26.) It might be objected, how will Believers then escape more than others; for none of them continue in all that is written in the Law: The Apostle here obviateth this Objection, by telling the <ns0:hi>Galatians,</ns0:hi> that as to Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lievers Christ had <ns0:hi>redeemed them from this curse.</ns0:hi> The word gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rally signifies <ns0:hi>delivering</ns0:hi>; here it signifies a deliverance <ns0:hi>by a price paid.</ns0:hi> This was</ns0:note>, by being made a curse for us <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">by <ns0:hi>being himself made a curse for us</ns0:hi>; not only execrable to men, but bearing the wrath and indignation of God due for sin: For so it was written, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 21.23.</ns0:note>, for it is written, cursed <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> every one that hangeth on a tree <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>He that is hanged is accursed of God</ns0:hi>; that is, hath born the wrath or curse of God due to him for his sin: The Apostle applying this to Christ teacheth us, that Christ also hanging upon the Cross, bare the curse of God due to the sins of Believers; in whose stead, as well as for who<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e good and benefit, he dyed. And indeed he could no otherway redeem believers from the curse of the Law, but by being made himself a curse for them, some think, that under the Law he who was hanged was made a curse, not only politically, but typically; as signifying that curse which Christ should be made on the behalf of the Elect.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Apostle, by <ns0:hi>the blessing of Abraham,</ns0:hi> here understands those spiritual blessings of <ns0:hi>Iustification, Reconciliation,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Adop<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion,</ns0:hi> which came to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> upon his believing, and the im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />putation of righteousness thereupon unto him. Christ (he saith) was made <ns0:hi>a curse</ns0:hi> for us, that all those blessings through him might come on the Gentiles; and so all the Nations of the Earth might be blessed in him. Particularly</ns0:note>, that we might receive the promise of the spirit through faith <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">that the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> might receive the <ns0:hi>promise of the Spirit</ns0:hi>; which promise is not to be interpreted so narrowly, as only to signifie its miraculous gifts, but to be extended to all those gifts and habits of grace which are the effects of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lievers, whether sanctifying or sealing them; which Holy Spirit is received upon persons believing: See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 4.6. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Brethren, I speak after the manner of men, <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 9.17.</ns0:note> though it be but a mans <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>testament.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> covenant <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The word here translated <ns0:hi>Covenant,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is ordinarily translated <ns0:hi>Testament; Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.28. It signifies in the general, an ordering or disposing of things; more specially, a <ns0:hi>Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment</ns0:hi>; which is the disposition of the <ns0:hi>Testators goods</ns0:hi> after his Death. Now (saith the Apostle) I here argue according to the ordinary methods and doings of men; who have such a respect for a mans Testament; as that</ns0:note>, yet if it be confirmed <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">if it be once confir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med, according to the methods of Law and civil S<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>nctions of men, or rather by the <ns0:hi>Death of the Testator,</ns0:hi> (for a <ns0:hi>Testament is of no force while the Testator liveth</ns0:hi>;) nor will men alter the Will or last Testament of a deceased person, though it be not as yet confirmed according to the methods of hum<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ne Laws.</ns0:note>, no man disanulleth or addeth thereunto <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>No man,</ns0:hi> that is no just man, will go about to disanul it, or add to it, nor will any just Government endure any such violation of it. Hence the Apostle argueth, both the certainty and inalterableness of the <ns0:hi>Covenant of Grace with Abraham,</ns0:hi> and until the death of Christ it was but a Covenant, or a Testament not fully confirmed, but yet inalterable, because the Covenant of that God who cannot ly, nor repent, but by the death of Christ it became a <ns0:hi>Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment,</ns0:hi> and a Testament ratified and confirmed by the Death of the person that was the Testator; therefore never to be disa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nulled, never capable of any additions. Those words, <ns0:hi>nor ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deth thereto,</ns0:hi> are fitly added, because these false Teachers, though they might pretend not to disanul Gods Covenant, hold<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing still Justification by Christ; yet they <ns0:hi>added thereto,</ns0:hi> making <ns0:hi>circumcision,</ns0:hi> and other legal observances necessary to Justifica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion; whereas by Gods Covenant or <ns0:hi>Testament,</ns0:hi> confirmed now by the Death of Christ, <ns0:hi>Faith in Christ</ns0:hi> only was necessary.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 17.7. ver. 8.</ns0:note> to Abraham, and his seed were the promises made <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The promises, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 12.3. <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 22.18. In the one of which places it is said, <ns0:hi>In thee</ns0:hi>; in the other, <ns0:hi>in thy seed shall all the Nations of the Earth be blessed.</ns0:hi> He saith, <ns0:hi>promises,</ns0:hi> either be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause of the repetition of the same promises, or taking in also other promises.</ns0:note>, he saith not as of seeds as to many, but as of one, and to thy seed, which was Christ <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Some may object against the Apostles con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clusion, that the promise respected only one, and that was Christ; because <ns0:hi>God said not seeds of many, but seed:</ns0:hi> whereas the Term <ns0:hi>Seed</ns0:hi> is a Noun of multitude, and signifieth more than one: Besides that the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word which is used <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.18. ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitteth not the <ns0:hi>Plural number.</ns0:hi> But it is answered, That though the word translated <ns0:hi>seed,</ns0:hi> admitteth not the <ns0:hi>Plu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral Number</ns0:hi> yet had God intended more than <ns0:hi>one,</ns0:hi> he could have expressed it by words, signifying <ns0:hi>Children,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rations, &c.</ns0:hi> 2. That the Term <ns0:hi>Seed,</ns0:hi> though a Noun of multitude, yet is often applyed to a single person; as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 3.15. (where it also signifieth Christ;) <ns0:hi>Se<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>h</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>another seed, Gen.</ns0:hi> 4.25. (and so in many other places.) Some think that by <ns0:hi>Seed</ns0:hi> he meaneth Believers, and so interpret it of <ns0:hi>Christ mystical.</ns0:hi> And that the scope of the Apostle in this place is to prove, that both the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> were to be justified the same way; because they were justified in force, and by vertue of the promise, which was not made to many, but to <ns0:hi>one Church,</ns0:hi> which was to consist both of <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> for (according to the prophesie of <ns0:hi>Cajaphas, Ioh.</ns0:hi> 11.52.) Christ dyed, <ns0:hi>that he might gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.</ns0:hi> The promises made to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> were but the <ns0:hi>exhibition</ns0:hi> of the Eternal Covenant of Grace, made between the <ns0:hi>Father,</ns0:hi> and his <ns0:hi>Son Christ Iesus,</ns0:hi> (who was in it both the <ns0:hi>Media<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tor</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Surety</ns0:hi>;) which Covenant was promulged, as to <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> so to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>; in these words, <ns0:hi>In thy seed shall all the Nations of the Earth be called,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>in Christ.</ns0:hi> From whence the Apostle proveth, that there is no <ns0:hi>justification by the works of the Law,</ns0:hi> but in, and by Christ, and the exercise of Faith in him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And this I say, that the covenant that was before confirmed of God<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> in Christ <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The word translated <ns0:hi>Covenant,</ns0:hi> is the same as before; ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />narily signifying ones disposal of things in his last Will and Testament. Which name is given to the Covenant of Grace, with respect to the Death of Christ; for though Christ as yet had not dyed, yet he was, by vertue of the Covenant of Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demption, and in Gods counsels, <ns0:hi>The Lamb slain from the founda<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of the World, Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.8. This (he saith) was <ns0:hi>in Christ,</ns0:hi> (as <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> promised seed,) confirmed of God to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> by Gods Oath, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 17, 18. by frequent repetitions of it, by such solemn Rites as covenants use to be confirmed by, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15.17, 18. By the Seals of Circumcision, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17.11: <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.11. By a long prescription, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> though it received indeed its final and ultimate consummation by the Death of Christ, yet it was before many wayes confirmed.</ns0:note>, the law <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 12.40, 41.</ns0:note> which was four hundred and thirty years af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, cannot disanul <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Law was given 430 years after the giving this promise to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> though <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15.13. the round number of 400 years only be mentioned: which are to be counted from the birth of <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi>; yet <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 12.40. they are reckoned (as here) 430 years, from <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> going out of <ns0:hi>Canaan, Gen.</ns0:hi> 12.4. from whence to the birth of <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> were 25 years; <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 21.5. compared with <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 12.4. From the birth of <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> till <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> was born, 60 years, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 25.26. From thence till <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> went down into <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> 130; <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47.9. where they abode 215 years.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 4.13, 14.</ns0:note> that it should make the promise of no effect <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Hence the Apostle concludes, that it was impossible that the <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> which was not given till 430 years after the confirmation of the promise, should make the promise confirmed of no ef<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:479" />18 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 8.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> if the inheritance <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> of the law, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> no more of promise <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">If the Inheritance of the Heavenly <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> typified by the Earthly <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> the promise of which was made to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> be to be obtained by the fulfilling the Law, and yielding obedience to it, then 'tis no more of the promise. It is much the same with what the Apostle said before, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.14. and with what he had said, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.6. <ns0:hi>If by grace, then it is no more of works, otherwise, grace is no more grace: But if it be of works,</ns0:hi> then it is <ns0:hi>no more grace; otherwise work is no more work.</ns0:hi> He shews, that there is an opposition betwixt <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Work,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Promise</ns0:hi>; That which is of <ns0:hi>grace,</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:hi>promise,</ns0:hi> is of free love; That which is of works, and the Law, is wages, and a <ns0:hi>reward of Debt.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, but God gave <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> to Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham by promise <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">But (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>God gave the inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritance to Abraham by promise</ns0:hi>; he of his free love ingaging him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self thereunto.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Wherefore then <ns0:hi>serveth</ns0:hi> the law <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Some might say, to what purpose was the Law given, as if there could be no use of it unless it were available to Justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fication.</ns0:note>? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 15.22. Rom. 4.15. & 5.20. & 7.8.</ns0:note> it was added because of transgressions <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">It was (saith the Apostle) given after the promise, not to supply something wanting as to Justification, to prescribe some works that must be added; but either to restrain sin, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.9. or to shew and discover sin, to make men see that they stood in need of Christ, vid. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.13.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Till <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> the promised Seed should come, who <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.4. <ns0:hi>is the end of the Law for righteousness to every one that believeth</ns0:hi>; upon whose coming the Law contained in Ordinances ceased. That Christ is here to be understood by the <ns0:hi>Seed,</ns0:hi> is plain by the addition, to <ns0:hi>whom the promise was made.</ns0:hi> Some here understand by the <ns0:hi>Seed,</ns0:hi> Christ and the Church, (which both make up <ns0:hi>Christ mystical</ns0:hi>;) and interpret this Text by <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.14. till the Jews and Gentiles should be both made one.</ns0:note>, till the seed should come, to whom the promise was made <ns0:hi>u, and it was</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 7.53.</ns0:note> ordained by angels <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">This Law (he saith) <ns0:hi>was ordained by Angels,</ns0:hi> that when <ns0:hi>Luke, Acts</ns0:hi> 7.38. speaks of the Law as published by one Angel. The Apostle, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.2. calls it, <ns0:hi>the word sp<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ken by Angels.</ns0:hi> We read of no Angels, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19. <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 20. nor of any of the Saints; yet <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33.2. <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> saith God came from <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>Ten Thou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sand Saints.</ns0:hi> The Law was given either by the Ministry of an Angel, or by God attended with Angels.</ns0:note> in the hand <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 1.17. 1 Tim. 2.5.</ns0:note> of a mediator <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>In the hand,</ns0:hi> that is, (say some) under the Power of Christ the Mediator; but by the <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> is rather to be understood <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> which agreeth with <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 5.5. where <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> telleth the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> that he <ns0:hi>stood be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />twixt the Lord and them at that time, to shew them the word of the Lord,</ns0:hi> Nor is Christ any where called the <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Old,</ns0:hi> but of the <ns0:hi>New Testament, Heb.</ns0:hi> 8.6. and 12.24.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 Now a mediatour is not a <ns0:hi>mediatour</ns0:hi> of one, but God is one <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This is a Text acknowledged by all Interpreters to be ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry obscure; not so much as considered in it self, (for all know, that a <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> speaks one that goes in the middle, betwixt two persons that are at odds; so <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>annot be of one;) as in regard of the connexion of it with what went before; where he had told us, that the Law was given <ns0:hi>in the hand of a Mediator.</ns0:hi> There are various senses given of this verse, and the variety much ariseth from mens different understanding of the <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> in whose hand the Law was given. To me the Apostle seems to magnifie the <ns0:hi>Promise</ns0:hi> above the <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> in that the promise was given to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> immediately by God (<ns0:hi>who is one</ns0:hi> in essence) but the Law was given not immediately by God, but by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Media<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tor,</ns0:hi> who in that action was a Type of Christ. And God there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by shewed, that the Law would bring no man to Life and Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation without the one, and only Mediator Christ Jesus. Christ indeed is the <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>New Testament,</ns0:hi> he mediated for it, he mediateth in it; but it was mens transgression of the law that brought them in need of a Mediator, (sin being the only thing that separateth between God and Man.) <ns0:hi>God is one</ns0:hi>; and there had been no need of mediating between him and man, but for the Law which man had transgressed. Those that by the Mediator, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 19. understand <ns0:hi>Christ,</ns0:hi> make this the sense: That as a <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> supposeth two parties at odds, so Christs be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> speaks him to have respect to Jews and Gentiles. But this Interpretation seems to make Christ the <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> whom (the Apostle saith) he made <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>th one breaking down the partition wall, Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.14. But we do not find the name of <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> upon this account any where given unto Christ Many other senses are given, but the first mentio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned seemeth the most probable, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> that God made use of no Mediator in giving the promise, but only in giving the Law, which evidenced that Justification was not to be by it; nor had there been need of a true Mediator under the Gospel, but for the Law; mens transgression of which brought in a need of a Mediator; which proved that Justification could not be by the Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> the law then against the promises of God? God forbid <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Though it be thus, yet there is no such opposition be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />twixt the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Promises,</ns0:hi> as that either of them make the other useless. Far be it from me (saith the Apostle) to assert any such thing! they are not contrary to one another, but subservient to one another.</ns0:note>, for if there had been a law given which could have given life <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For if there had been <ns0:hi>a Law,</ns0:hi> which could by our perfect performance of it, have gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven us <ns0:hi>a righteousness,</ns0:hi> wherein we might have stood righteous before God:</ns0:note>, verily righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness should have been by the law <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Then <ns0:hi>righteousness should have been by the Law</ns0:hi>; then men might have hoped to have been justified and accep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted of God by me for such obedience; then indeed the Law had been against the promises, they holding forth another righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Righteousness of God from Faith to Faith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 But the scripture <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 11.3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> hath concluded all un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der sin <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">It pleased God to give a Law, which if <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> had continu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in his estate of innocence, might have given life; God considering man in his lapsed state, that now is not possible, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.10. <ns0:hi>There is none righteous, no not one,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.3. <ns0:hi>We are all children of wrath.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That the promises of Life and Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation might be given to those, who, according to the new Covenant of the Gospel, should receive and accept of the Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diator, and the terms of Salvation which God offers to us in the Gospel; where these promises are exhibited upon conditi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of Believing. Though upon our first reflection upon it, it may seem strange to us, that God having in his Eternal coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sels fixed the Salvation of man upon a Covenant of Grace, and his believing in Jesus Christ, should in time first propound a Covenant of works, <ns0:hi>do this and live</ns0:hi>; yet upon our second thoughts this will appear necessary; For till man was a transgressor by breaking the Law, and violating the first Covenant, there was no room for a Mediator; no cause for mens applying them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves to a Mediator. God therefore first gave out the Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant of works, and suffered man to break it; and then he re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vealed the Mediator to lapsed man; that so they who should be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve in him might obtain the promise of life, to which by the fall they had forfeited their right.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 But before faith came <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Before the Covenant of Grace, or the Doctrine of the Gospel, or Christ himself was revealed.</ns0:note>, we were kept un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the law <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Apostle either speaks of all mankind; of whom it is true, that until Gods re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />velation of the Covenant of Grace, they had no other way of Salvation made known to them than by the Law of works, or else of the Jews; to whom, though before Christ there was a revelation of the Gospel, yet it was more dark and imperfect, so as they were kept under the Law; but few apprehending any other way of Justification, than by the works of the Law. But the Apostle saith they were but <ns0:hi>shut up under it</ns0:hi>; God never intended it, as that by the observance of which they should be saved; but as even then</ns0:note>, shut up unto the faith which should afterward be revealed <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">to those whom he intended to save, he made a more secret Revelation of his Gospel, so he had now more fully and plainly revealed the way of Salvation which he had from Eternity established.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Wherefore, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 10.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> the law <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Both the Law contained in Ordinances, and the moral Law,</ns0:note> was our school-master, <ns0:hi>to bring us</ns0:hi> unto Christ <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">was <ns0:hi>our School-master</ns0:hi>; serving us in the same stead that a School-master in a School doth, who only fitteth children for higher degrees of learning at Universities. The Ceremo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nial Law shewed us Christ in all his Types and Sacrifices; the <ns0:hi>Moral Law,</ns0:hi> shewed us the absolute need of a Mediator, as it shewed us sin; accused and condemned us for it; and it shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed us no help either for the guilt of sin contracted, or against the power of it.</ns0:note>, that we might be justified by faith <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">So that Gods end in giving us the law was that we might be fitted for Christ, and obtain Justification by believing in him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 But after that faith is come, we are no lon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger under a school-master <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">After that Christ, the object of saving Faith, was in the fulness of time revealed; and the Gospel, (which is the Doctrine of Faith,) was fully revealed and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ubl<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>shed, the time of our non-age was over.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:gap>. 4.5.</ns0:note> are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">All you that believe, whether Native Jews or Gentiles, are the children of God by Adoption through Faith in Jesus Christ. <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 1.12. so that you need not run back to the Law to look for help and Salvation from that; but only look unto Christ, to whom the Law was but a School-master to lead you, who being fully and clearly revealed, you may have immediate recourse to, by Faith; and need not to make use of the Jewish School-master, as hoping for Justification from the observan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces of the Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note>, have put on Christ <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Of those thus baptized, he saith, that <ns0:hi>they had put on Christ</ns0:hi>; they had accepted of, and received Christ for their <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
